articles.title: “Sit Nice!”: Peer Culture, Teacher Capacity, and Joint Socialization Efforts in Preschool
articles.abstract: Preschools instill soft skills that are crucial to children’s life outcomes. As preschool access expands, research and policy often focus on improving teacher quality. This focus downplays how much teachers’ efforts may depend on children’s peers. Drawing on two years of ethnography, I highlight two important aspects of socialization: teachers’ capacity to deliver messages in the moment, and peers’ tendency to support those messages. I compare socialization processes at two race- and class-segregated preschools. Three interrelated classroom conditions—children’s enrollment, attendance, and challenging behaviors—mattered for socialization interactions. Teachers at both preschools pursued socialization goals of instilling safe and formal classroom behaviors. At the affluent, majority-White preschool, teachers had a greater capacity to coach children in the moment, and peers had a culture of supporting teacher messages. At the low-income, racially diverse preschool, children placed the authority to coach classroom behavior in their teachers, who were pressed for time. I argue that socialization agents jointly influence behavior. In segregated preschools, teachers may shape classroom behavior to unequal extents, preventing early learning settings from disrupting future inequalities.

articles.title: Merit or Whiteness? Tracing Racial Bias in the Selection of Individual UN Human Rights Experts
articles.abstract: Do race or merit make an international expert? While existing research has uncovered epistemic biases related to gender and professions, racial bias in international organisations’ expert selection has not been captured. We argue that signalling whiteness is central to the certification of expertise because expert status is built on racialised structures of epistemic power. Examining individual-level data from 2,053 applications and selection outcomes across several stages in 124 decision rounds between 2011 and 2024 for the United Nations’ Special Procedures, we show that expert selection is subject to racial bias when candidates are chosen for in-person interviews and how markers of whiteness and merit overlap. We also find that non-white experts can increase their chances of being selected when they possess higher merit-related credentials than their white counterparts. Our research informs scholarship on racism in international relations, the production of expertise in international organisations, and human rights politics.

articles.title: Regional Deprivation, Individual Prospects, and Political Resentment
articles.authors: Giovanni Facchini, Anja Neundorf, Sergi Pardos-Prado, Cecilia Testa
articles.abstract: Regional economic conditions are well-established determinants of the geography of political resentment. However, regions are not homogeneous, and the mechanisms through which local economies affect individual political attitudes are unclear. We argue that feelings of relative deprivation are shaped by how personal prospects are tied to regional conditions, and that the interaction between subjective individual and regional deprivation affects perceptions of shared struggle and systemic unfairness. Through a large-scale survey experiment in Britain addressing geographical self-selection, we provide causal evidence that poor individuals in poor regions express political resentment, whereas in affluent regions the political attitudes of poor and wealthy individuals are indistinguishable. Our findings stress (1) the importance of egocentric mechanisms whereby local economies shape individual prospects; (2) the significance of subjective beliefs over objective information on deprivation; (3) the mobilization potential of highlighting regional deprivation by political entrepreneurs; and (4) the relevance of place-based policies to mitigate political discontent.

articles.title: Breaking into the Public Sphere: How Protest Tactics Shape Media Visibility
articles.abstract: Getting heard is a crucial first step for protesters to influence policy and public opinion. How can protest organisers boost their coverage in the media? This study provides new evidence on this question, based on a decade of UK environmental and economic protests from 2010 to 2020 ( N = 1,708). Relying on protest groups’ social media streams as trace data, I introduce a computer-assisted method for constructing a media-independent protest event dataset. Using a ‘within-group’ design, I provide a sharper test of the causal effects of tactical choices compared to previous studies. I find that confrontational elements, such as disruption and arrests, are the strongest predictors, more than doubling the expected magnitude of coverage. I also find that right-leaning (ideologically unsympathetic) outlets are more responsive to confrontational elements than left-leaning (ideologically sympathetic) outlets, which suggests that disruptive tactics affect the composition as well as the size of a protest’s audience.

articles.title: Who Benefits from Forbearance? Middle Classes and the Distributional Consequences of Informality
articles.abstract: Why do urban informal economies persist in middle-income democracies, even when legal frameworks mandate formalization? This article identifies the demand-side micro-foundations of selective non-enforcement, documenting how middle-class consumers benefit from informality and resist bearing the costs of formalization. Drawing on original survey data (n=1,568 and n=770) and five embedded survey experiments conducted in Buenos Aires, Argentina, it shows that middle-class voters benefit materially from informal labor and housing arrangements and oppose formalization when compliance imposes direct material costs. Support for formalization declines significantly when framed as raising taxes, increasing prices, or disrupting domestic labor supply. These findings challenge the view of informality as a survival mechanism for the poor alone, highlighting instead how middle-class consumption and cost preferences could play into the politics of forbearance.

articles.title: Selective Recommendation and Credible Exaggeration in Multidimensional Communication
articles.abstract: A sender who wants a receiver to acquire items regardless of quality cannot communicate credibly about one item, but with several she can, by recommending weakly better items. We characterise a continuum of selective recommendation equilibria combining partial statements with full statements recommending everything. Recommendations in partial statements are always followed; those in full statements are followed probabilistically, leaving senders indifferent. Full statements remain credible despite recommending bad items—what we call credible exaggeration. In experiments, senders use partial statements selectively alongside full statements; receivers follow nearly all recommendations in partial statements and almost half in full statements, transmitting information.

articles.title: A Signal-Extraction Theory of Inflation Pass-Through
articles.abstract: I develop a theory of state-dependent signal extraction in price setting. Firms infer how much sectoral price movements reflect persistent aggregate or transitory sector-specific disturbances. When inflation is low relative to sectoral variation, sticky-price firms discount competitor movements because following transitory movements risks leaving them mispriced. As inflation rises relative to sectoral noise, firms increasingly attribute these movements to aggregate shocks and sticky firms respond more strongly. UK micro-price data support these predictions: below approximately 1.9% sectoral inflation, sticky firms respond less to competitors than flexible firms; above it, the gap closes. This convergence generates state-dependent aggregate inflation dynamics.

articles.title: Relational Mechanisms in Trafficking Processes: Trust, Obligation and Controlled Dependence Across Stages in Ghana and Nigeria
articles.abstract: Human trafficking in West Africa is deeply connected to migration and labour markets, but existing studies often under‐specify the micro‐processes through which trafficking is organized. This study examines human trafficking in Ghana and Nigeria as a relational process facilitated by brokerage, obligation, and managed trust, with particular attention to how these mechanisms change across trafficking stages. This study used a concurrent mixed‐methods design, guided by critical realism and pragmatic methodological pluralism. Survey data were collected from 103 adults with trafficking, smuggling or mixed migration and exploitation experiences in Ghana ( n = 68) and Nigeria ( n = 33); two Cameroonian cases were retained for pooled description only and excluded from all Ghana‐Nigeria comparisons. Qualitative data were generated with 32 participants through in‐depth interviews, key informant interviews and four focus group discussions, and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Quantitative analysis was conducted in Stata 17.0. Recruitment was primarily facilitated by individual recruiters, often described as agents or brokers, although ties to friends and family remained substantial. This points to a mixed recruitment ecology in which social proximity legitimizes offers while brokerage enables them. Most recruiters were locally embedded, underlining the importance of local credibility in building trust. Exploitation was predominantly carried out by actors with whom participants reported no prior relationship, indicating role separation between recruiters and exploiters.

articles.title: Household Determinants of Migration and Remittances in Nepal: Evidence of a Poverty–Mobility Paradox
articles.abstract: This paper examines the determinants of household migration and remittance inflows in Nepal using panel data from the Nepal Household Risk and Vulnerability Survey (2016–2018). Departing from studies that examine migration and remittances separately, it employs a Heckman two‐step selection model to account for non‐random selection into migration. Consistent with the New Economics of Labour Migration, larger households and those with higher dependency ratios are more likely to send migrants, whereas poverty is negatively associated with migration, a pattern indicative of the poverty–mobility paradox; this negative association holds in all provinces and is statistically significant in Madhesh, Karnali and Sudurpashchim. Migration networks and digital connectivity are also positively associated with migration. Conditional on migration, remittance inflows are higher in larger households, households with higher dependency burdens, more assets and access to formal credit and lower where migration costs are higher. The results also reveal substantial provincial heterogeneity. The findings highlight the importance of financial inclusion, lower migration costs and improved digital infrastructure for enhancing the developmental benefits of migration.

articles.title: The Dependence Dilemma: Engagement, Vulnerability, and the Politics of Derisking
articles.authors: Brett V. Benson, Haonan Dong, Bradley C. Smith
articles.abstract: What makes economic interdependence a force for peace rather than a source of strategic vulnerability? We argue that interdependence generates both pacifying opportunity costs and dangerous dependence, and the tension between these two forces is the key to understanding when economic engagement promotes peace and when it provokes war. We develop a dynamic model of economic dependence and conflict that generates both the pacifying and conflict-inducing effects of interdependence within a single unified framework. We show that states use “derisking” as a strategic middle path, selectively restricting economic engagement to reset future leverage without destroying the gains from exchange that make peace valuable. The theory explains why dependence-driven wars are rare yet possible. Forward-looking leaders prefer incurring the costs of economic restraint to the catastrophic risks of conflict. When derisking is structurally foreclosed or restrictions destroy too much economic value, the commitment problem cannot be managed through policy and preventive war may occur.

articles.title: Territory Without Centralization: Conflicting Spatial Ideologies of the Shogunate, Domains, and Villages in Early Modern Japan
articles.abstract: This article reconceptualizes the formation of territory by examining early modern Japan, showing that territory can emerge through bottom-up processes without centralization. Contrary to dominant narratives based on European history that portray territory as a product of top-down projects, the Japanese case reveals that multiple levels of political actors—the Tokugawa shogunate, individual domains, and village communities—held competing spatial ideologies and engaged in struggles over how space should be organized and governed, and as a result, territory emerged without centralization. The shogunate sought to impose a vision of a unified territory through land surveys and repeated production of provincial maps. However, because it lacked the capacity to carry out these projects directly, implementation depended on domains, inadvertently strengthening their territorial demarcation and autonomy. Yet domains themselves could not fully impose their spatial conceptions onto the population. Because land surveys focused only on cultivated fields, the delineation of boundaries in uncultivated areas was driven by peasants whose need for access to common resources such as grasslands and timber motivated numerous inter-village disputes. Through boundary disputes, villages played a central role in defining the borders that ultimately structured domanial territories. This article contributes to international relations scholarship by revising the dominant state-centric view of territory and state formation, casting doubt on the effectiveness of war making and map making in the process of state formation, demonstrating that territorial formation need not coincide with sovereignty, and advancing our understanding of non-European historical international order.

articles.title: Slow Heart that Matters in Seeing Wars: Cost Perceptions and Negative Emotions of Seeing Human Death in the War Zones
articles.authors: Atsushi Tago, Toshiyuki Himichi, Megumi Kato, Shihoko Makino, Nobuhiro Mifune
articles.abstract: There has been a significant rise in the presence of war imagery in our daily lives in recent years. The ongoing conflict in Ukraine, along with hostilities involving the USA, Israel, Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran has led to news broadcasts frequently showcasing scenes of urban destruction, injured civilians, explosions, artillery fire, missile strikes, and casualties. Additionally, the internet is filled with numerous graphic images, prompting some experts to argue that such visuals can trigger trauma or at least cause a significant negative affect. This article seeks to investigate how these images shape individual perceptions of the costs of warfare through physiological experiments of the college students sample. The research examines how we see the graphical material and have an emotional reaction against war, utilizing electrocardiogram (ECG) data and six basic emotion questions. The research reveals that visuals of fallen war victims enhance the overall understanding of the costs associated with war, eliciting multiple negative feelings (we call it Type 2 Negative Emotions) in viewers.

articles.title: Knowledge gaps and scientific progress
articles.authors: Kara Kedrick, Wenlong Yang, Thomas Gebhart, Yang Wang, Russell J. Funk
articles.abstract: Knowledge production is often viewed as an endogenous process in which discovery arises through the recombination of existing theories, findings, and concepts. Yet not all recombinations are equally valuable, and identifying those that may prove most generative remains challenging. We propose that a crucial form of recombination occurs when linking concepts creates knowledge gaps—empty regions in the conceptual landscape that may focus scientific attention on unexplored connections. Using computational topology, we develop a method to identify knowledge gaps in science at scale. In this framework, gaps form when new connections complete cycles in evolving networks of scientific concepts. We apply the method to 34,363,623 papers in Microsoft Academic Graph spanning 1900 to 2020. The main analyses use samples ranging from 8,643,571 to 31,983,201 papers. Compared with papers that introduce novel concept pairs without opening gaps, gap-opening papers have greater long-term citation impact, are more disruptive of prior work, and exhibit greater delayed recognition. Gap-opening papers receive fewer citations within five years of publication but more over twenty years, consistent with scientific communities needing time to recognize and develop newly opened research territories. Evidence for the generative capacity of gap-opening papers—as indicated by high citation impact and disruption—replicates in five additional databases (OpenAlex, the PubMed Knowledge Graph, Dimensions, American Physical Society journals, and United States patents) and across eight concept vocabularies, including several derived directly from text. Together, these results point to a distinctive generative role for gap opening in scientific discovery.

articles.title: Promises and pitfalls of community moderation on social media
articles.authors: Isabelle Augenstein, Michiel A. Bakker, Tanmoy Chakraborty, David Corney, Emilio Ferrara, Iryna Gurevych, Scott Hale, Eduard Hovy, Heng Ji, Irene Larraz, Filippo Menczer, Preslav Nakov, Paolo Papotti, Dhruv Sahnan, Greta Warren, Giovanni Zagni
articles.abstract: Social media platforms have traditionally relied on internal moderation teams and partnerships with independent fact-checking organizations to identify and flag problematic content. Recently, however, platforms including X (formerly Twitter) and Meta have shifted toward community-driven content moderation by launching their own versions of crowd-sourced fact-checking—Community Notes. If effectively scaled and governed, such crowd-checking initiatives have the potential to combat misinformation as successfully as community-driven efforts once did with spam. However, moderating misinformation is inherently more complex: perceptions of truth are often shaped by personal biases, political leanings, and cultural contexts, complicating consensus on what constitutes misleading content. This suggests that community efforts, while valuable, cannot replace the indispensable role of professional fact-checkers. Here we explore the emerging role of community-driven moderation, critically evaluate both the promises and the challenges of Community Notes at scale, and identify how collaborative and technical innovations can integrate the two distinct approaches.

articles.title: Humans show limited ability to distinguish human-authored from AI-generated political content on social media
articles.authors: Sejin Paik, Tiago Ventura, Rebecca Ansell, Leticia Bode, Autumn Toney-Wails, Lisa Singh
articles.abstract: This study employs a set of behavioral experiments to examine how individuals perceive the humanness of social media posts about the 2024 U.S. presidential debate between Kamala Harris and Donald Trump. Posts presented in the experiment were authored either by humans or chatbots, varying the large language model (LLM), the model architecture, the social media platform, and the political personas. Participants judged randomly paired posts to identify which they perceived to be AI-generated. We find that human-authored posts were on average perceived as more human-like than AI outputs generated from five of the six LLMs in this study. However, participants’ ability to detect AI-generated content is limited. They do so only slightly above chance in human–AI pairs, and this ability weakens for newer LLMs, varies by platform, and reflects partisan bias. Only posts generated with Llama 3.3 scored, on average, higher on perceived humanness than human-authored posts. The social media platform also mattered, with participants distinguishing human from AI on most platforms (YouTube, TikTok, Truth Social), but not on X/Twitter. Incivility and negative emotions are associated with high humanness perceptions, and partisan identity also shaped evaluations, with Republican respondents more likely to view ideologically misaligned AI posts as AI-generated.

articles.title: Rethinking broad diet breadth as a sign of scarcity: A 50,000-y record of subsistence from northwestern Australia
articles.authors: Tiina Manne, Erin Mein, Jane Balme, Sue O’Connor, Ken Aplin, Peter Veth
articles.abstract: The prey choice model, widely applied in archaeological reconstructions of Pleistocene diet, predicts that people will initially focus on a narrow suite of high-ranked prey before broadening their diet to include lower-ranked species as necessitated by subsistence needs. However, evidence from arid and semiarid northern Australia challenges this assumption. Archaeological faunal records demonstrate that a broad diet was established early and persisted through the Holocene. We argue that these diverse diets do not indicate resource scarcity, but rather represent an ideal strategy for exploiting abundant, low-risk hidden, or cryptic prey, as well as high-risk, conspicuous prey within an environment characterized by unpredictable rainfall. This pattern also necessitates reconceptualizing traditional notions of prey rank and dietary breadth. Rather than adhering to static prey rankings, northern Australian peoples skillfully adapted their hunting strategies in response to fluctuating nutritional content and pursuit costs of different species. The most successful subsistence strategy in this region was therefore one of high responsiveness and flexibility, manifesting as a consistently broad diet. This case study suggests that the relationship between human dietary breadth and resource abundance is more nuanced in situations of abundant, cryptic prey.

articles.title: Reducing belief in conspiracy theories as they unfold using large language models
articles.authors: Thomas H. Costello, Nathaniel Rabb, Michael Nicholas Stagnaro, Gordon Pennycook, David G. Rand
articles.abstract: The emergence of conspiracy theories in the wake of major events is a significant societal challenge. Here, we test whether conversational dialogues with a large language model (LLM) can reduce belief in immediately unfolding conspiracies. In experiments conducted in the days following the July 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump and the September 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk, US adults (Experiment 1: N = 472; Experiment 2: N = 1,042) holding conspiratorial views about the crisis event engaged in a multiturn conversation with an LLM prompted to reduce their conspiracy belief. Compared to control participants who either discussed an irrelevant topic with an LLM or viewed a static fact sheet, participants in the LLM treatment showed significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs in both experiments. We also found suggestive evidence of downstream effects of the LLM treatment, observing reduced belief in some—but not all—analyses of different conspiratorial beliefs 1 to 2 mo later. These results shed light on the psychology of emerging conspiracies and highlight the potential for scalable, information-focused LLM interventions to counteract misinformation in the immediate aftermath of high-profile societal events.

articles.title: Cognitive diversity and majority rule
articles.authors: Lu Hong, P. J. Lamberson, Scott E. Page, Ville A. Satopää
articles.abstract: Societies rely on groups–boards, panels, committees, and representative bodies–to make important decisions for good reason: overwhelming evidence shows groups usually make more accurate choices than individuals. The predominant logic for group accuracy rests on reasoning formulated in the Condorcet Jury Theorem, which states that if voters receive independent and equally accurate generated signals, majority rule produces decisions that i) are more accurate than the average voter, ii) improve in individual accuracy and iii) group size, and iv) approach perfect accuracy as group size becomes large. An alternative logic based on interpreted signals explains the accuracy of majority rule as arising from the aggregation of diverse mental models. Group accuracy results from the same state of the world being classified differently by different people. In this framework, the set of possible group accuracies can be characterized conditional on average individual accuracy and average pairwise diversity. Majority rule groups are only guaranteed to outperform their members when diversity is high. Using data from a variety of empirical settings, along with simulations of a minimal nearest-neighbor model, we find much stronger support for the predictions of the interpreted signals framework than for the standard generated signals model. We further show empirical evidence for a diversity–accuracy paradox, in which more diverse groups are less accurate unless average individual accuracy is nearly constant across groups. Our findings have important implications for group composition and institutional and organizational design as well as for the potential gains from deliberation.

articles.title: Opinion formation through popular votes: Elite cues and polarization in EU referendums
articles.authors: Nelly Buntfuß, Felix Grünewald, Arndt Leininger
articles.abstract: Referendums are often seen as instruments to enhance the legitimacy of political decisions. However, rather than assuming that referendums merely aggregate citizens’ preferences, we conceptualize them as arenas of opinion formation. We examine this dynamic in three studies of national referendums on European integration. First, time-series cross-sectional analyses of Eurobarometer data from 15 countries (1973–2012) show that European Union referendums increase the proportion of citizens who have an opinion on the European Union. Second, analyses of a broader set of referendum outcomes demonstrate that public opinion, revealed through these outcomes, reacts to elite cues. Third, panel surveys from two European Union membership referendums trace opinion formation at the individual level. Together, these findings demonstrate that referendums not only allow citizens to voice their opinions on important issues but also provide a venue for these opinions to develop. Under certain conditions, referendums can also intensify political divisions on these issues.

articles.title: The diffusion of LGBTQ policies in the American states
articles.abstract: This article examines the factors influencing state-level adoption of LGBTQ (lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer) policies in the United States over the past three decades, focusing on both expansive and restrictive policies. Public opinion and policy on LGBTQ rights have shifted dramatically, with many changes occurring at the state level. Using a unique dataset of nearly 800 policy adoptions, I apply pooled event history analysis models to assess the role of policy diffusion, party control, and the initiative process. The results show that states are more likely to adopt LGBTQ policies when co-partisan states have done so, but this effect diminishes over time, indicating policy imitation. In addition, higher initiative usage is associated with increased adoption of expansive policies. These findings suggest that the dramatic increase in policymaking in this area is being driven by a desire for states to symbolically display their values rather than waiting to see the effect of policy adoption and suggest the policy network will remain heavily polarized by party control in the coming years.

articles.title: Beyond ruler and ruled: Legitimacy, power differences, and plebeian responses to resurgent oligarchy
articles.abstract: Political legitimacy is typically understood as constituted by a dyadic relationship between ruler and ruled. Realist theories of legitimacy retain this dyadic conceptualization. This is problematic for two reasons: it underplays the normative implications of power differences among the ruled and, as such, limits students of politics’ capacity to make evaluative claims about the link between legitimacy and democracy amid resurgent oligarchic power. Developing underspecified insights from Bernard Williams and Philip Pettit helps address both problems. First, foregrounding power differences between rulers and the ruled and among the ruled allows a tripartite conceptual distinction in theorizing legitimacy in modern rule of law states: between elite rulers and two categories of the ruled, oligarchic and ordinary citizens. Second, drawing on this tripartite distinction to distinguish two contemporary scenarios of oligarchic resurgence spells out its evaluative usefulness, especially regarding the applicability of plebeian responses and the relationship between legitimacy and democracy.

articles.title: Unequal Paths: How Spatial Opportunity and Affirmative Action Shape Social Mobility Among Ex-Untouchable Castes
articles.abstract: This article examines the pathways to upward social mobility for historically stigmatized groups, whose advancement is constrained by stigma, discrimination, and spatial segregation. While existing literatures on affirmative action and residential inequality offer valuable insights, they rarely speak to each other, leaving key mechanisms and intragroup disparities underexplored. I argue that historically contingent processes shape the organization of spatial opportunities within neighborhood environments. These opportunities in conjunction with affirmative action determine who achieves upward mobility. Drawing on a mixed-methods approach – including a unique dataset on the occupational class of disaggregated ex-untouchable castes, longue durée historical ethnography, interviews, and cartography – I compare mobility outcomes across twelve ex-untouchable castes in Ajmer, India. The case of the Kolis illustrates how a historically enriched residential environment enabled greater access to affirmative action and entry into the middle class.

articles.title: Corruption Perceptions, the Pendleton Act, and Sovereign Borrowing Costs
articles.authors: John A. Dove, Noah J. Trudeau
articles.abstract: Significant research suggests that systems of bureaucratic patronage tend to promote corruption and reduce the efficient production of publicly provided goods. However, much less work has been done to consider how market actors perceive such selection processes and especially reforms implemented to reduce such corruption. This study rectifies this by evaluating how the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act impacted federal borrowing costs. If patronage resulted in increased corruption and bureaucratic inefficiency, this should be reflected in relatively higher bond yields. If the Pendleton Act was successful in curbing this behavior, then this should be rewarded by market actors in the form of lower borrowing costs. Using interrupted time series analysis with and without control, we find that the passage of the Pendleton Act did, in fact, result in lower borrowing costs for the federal government of between 63 and 84 basis points depending on specification. Implications are discussed.

articles.title: Excessive Heat and Correctional Officer Turnover: Evidence From Texas
articles.abstract: Correctional work is difficult, dangerous, and hot. Many US prisons lack air‐conditioning, resulting in sweltering conditions for both incarcerated people and the street‐level bureaucrats tasked with their supervision. We examine the effect of working in the summer heat without air‐conditioning on correctional officer turnover using personnel records of nearly 60,000 Texas Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ) employees across 68 prisons between 2010 and 2023. We demonstrate that, among the least‐experienced frontline employees before the onset of COVID‐19, the difference in the probability of departing between those working in prisons without and with air‐conditioning is, on average, 0.33 percentage points larger in the hottest months than in the coolest—an approximately 12% change relative to the baseline departure rate. Back‐of‐the‐envelope estimates suggest that installing air‐conditioning to combat understaffing is comparable in cost to raising salaries, the TDCJ's standard response to high turnover.

articles.title: Quality Controls Can Improve the Replicability of Survey Experiments Using Online Nonprobability Panels
articles.authors: Edgar Cook, James Martherus, Alexander Podkul, Anja Kilibarda
articles.abstract: Scholars across multiple disciplines have documented challenges related to replicability, often referred to as a “replication crisis.” While a range of explanations exist, some have argued that the growing reliance on online nonprobability samples contributes to replication failures. At the same time, concerns have mounted regarding the quality of these samples, as inattentive, duplicate, or fraudulent respondents can bias estimates and diminish effect sizes. In this research note, we replicate three well-known survey experiments, using data collected from three separate online nonprobability panels (N = 6,000). We compare the “off-the-shelf” samples with subsets that pass a series of attention and fraud checks and that remove duplicate respondents. We find that all three experiments replicate in terms of direction and significance across the full samples, but in two out of three cases, effect magnitudes are replicated only once low-quality responses are removed.

articles.title: Mass Perceptions of Agency Ideology
articles.authors: Maxwell B Allamong, Manuel P Teodoro
articles.abstract: Federal agencies have become central actors in contemporary American politics, overseeing salient policy domains with clear ideological stakes. While scholars have long considered ideology as an important dimension of bureaucratic reputation, existing measures have largely relied on surveys of political elites or indicators such as employees’ campaign donations, leaving mass perceptions unexplored. Using data from a team module on the 2022 Cooperative Election Study, we provide descriptive evidence of the public’s perceptions of the ideological leanings of twelve federal agencies. We show that the public perceives meaningful ideological variation across agencies, with some seen as relatively more liberal (EPA), some more conservative (DOD), and others ideologically moderate (USPS). Additionally, mass perceptions of ideology closely align with measures derived from expert assessments, agency employees, or advanced computational approaches. They also correlate with partisanship, with Republicans (Democrats) rating agencies as relatively more liberal (conservative). Together, these findings establish ideology as a broadly perceptible, if partially variable, feature of government agencies, with potential to shape how citizens evaluate and interact with the American bureaucracy.

articles.title: International Power
articles.abstract: An interconnected world increases economic efficiency while giving certain countries leverage over others. We aim to describe and understand international power stemming from trade. Using an illustrative model of trade with possibilities of bilateral disputes and ex-post hold-ups, we highlight that bilateral asymmetry in import dependence can be a source of power towards one another. We construct the model-implied measure of international power — asymmetric bilateral import dependence, weighted inversely by sectoral trade elasticities — across country pairs over the past 20 years. Combining this measure with comprehensive data on bilateral engagement events and a high-frequency measure of bilateral geopolitical relationships, we examine the consequences and strategic causes of international power. We present two main empirical results. First, increases in international power between countries — which raise the credibility of threats of trade disruptions — induce more bilateral engagement and negotiations. Second, evidence suggests that worsened geopolitical relationships — in anticipation of future disputes — prompt countries to build up greater international power through adjusting trade activities.

articles.title: Generative AI And Creative Goods: Market Expansion, Crowd-Out, and Copyright
articles.authors: Samuel G Goldberg, H Tai Lam
articles.abstract: We study how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) affects creative goods markets using data from a large stock images marketplace. In December 2022, the platform announced it would allow artists to sell GenAI-produced images, subject to two conditions: all GenAI images must be labeled, and GenAI would be prohibited in certain markets. We exploit this policy variation using a difference-in-differences design. We estimate a 136% increase in image production and 47% increase in active artists, accompanied by a 15% decline in non-GenAI production and 29% decline in non-GenAI active artists. On the demand side, total sales increase by 82%, but non-GenAI sales fall by 28% and non-GenAI sales rates decline by 3 percentage points. We use image embeddings to develop novel measures of image quality, characteristics, and market composition.We find that quality (measured as predicted sales probability) increases by 9 percentage points overall and 2 percentage points for non-GenAI content, suggesting low-quality non-GenAI artists exit. Our product characteristic measures indicate that GenAI production is heavily concentrated in characteristic space, potentially limiting the value of these images to the market. Non-GenAI production responds to GenAI by differentiating into niches. We discuss implications for copyright policy and the longer-run sustainability of original creative work.

articles.title: Firms’ Perceived Cost of Capital
articles.abstract: We analyze firms’ perceptions of their cost of capital using hand-collected data. The perceived cost of capital is associated with the allocation of capital across firms. In a model with inefficient financial markets, firms can maximize their current market value by setting their perceived cost of capital equal to the expected returns on their debt and equity. In the data, little variation in firms’ perceived cost of capital can be justified by variation in expected returns, suggesting that firms do not follow this market-value maximization benchmark. Alternatively, firms may aim to maximize their “fair value” corrected for financial market inefficiencies. In the data, a fair-value benchmark (based on the CAPM) can justify half the variation in the perceived cost of capital. However, most of the variation can be justified by the beliefs of financial analysts about expected returns. Using a quantitative model, we find that the observed distortions in the perceived cost of capital can substantially impact capital allocation and thereby reduce aggregate productivity.

articles.title: Taxing Homeowners Who Can't or Won't Borrow
articles.abstract: Using high-frequency administrative data covering millions of US homeowners, I document three novel facts about homeowner responses to property tax increases driven by rising home values. First, non-migrating homeowners cut consumption, exhibit financial distress, and do not borrow against their higher home values. Second, heterogeneity analysis shows that consumption responses do not vary by liquidity, consistent with savings target behavior. In contrast, distress responses are concentrated among liquidity-constrained homeowners. Many homeowners report being debt averse and therefore unwilling to borrow in order to avoid illiquidity and distress. Third, tax hikes induce migration—partly by displacing illiquid homeowners—but do not accelerate neighborhood change. A simple welfare framework reveals that the largest costs of property taxes arise from financial distress, suggesting welfare gains from policies that limit taxes for liquidity-constrained households.

articles.title: Limits of Disclosure in Search Markets
articles.abstract: This paper examines competitive information disclosure in search markets with a mix of selective consumers, who search costlessly, and casual consumers, who incur positive search costs. Selective consumers incentivize truthful disclosure; casual consumers, concealment. With both types, the equilibrium features partial disclosure, which persists despite intense competition. Casual consumers may search actively, but only in small markets. While selective consumers benefit from increased competition, casual consumers may be harmed. Changes in search costs have non-monotone effects: the equilibrium approaches full disclosure as the cost approaches zero or the mean valuation. When costs are high, further increases raise equilibrium informativeness and the welfare of selective consumers, while reducing the welfare of casual consumers.

articles.title: Fine Stratification of Survey Experiments
articles.abstract: This paper studies a two-stage model of experimentation, where the researcher first samples representative experimental participants from an eligible pool, then assigns each sampled unit to treatment or control, using matched k-tuples randomization at both stages. To implement such designs, we develop a fast algorithm for matching units into k-tuples for any k ≥ 2 and any dimension of covariates. By surveying 200 recent experimental working papers, we estimate that our algorithm newly enables multivariate fine stratification with provable match quality guarantees in about 48% of recent papers. We show that finely stratified sampling and assignment both nonparametrically reduce the variance of treatment effect estimation, with the gains from stratified sampling increasing in the size of the eligible pool and how well covariates predict treatment effect heterogeneity. We develop new inference methods that fully exploit the efficiency gains from both design stages, allowing researchers to report smaller standard errors if they designed a representative experiment. An application to nine published experiments quantifies the efficiency gains.

articles.title: The Labor Demand and Labor Supply Channels of Monetary Policy
articles.authors: Sebastian Graves, Christopher Huckfeldt, Eric T Swanson
articles.abstract: Monetary policy is typically understood to affect employment through labor demand, with the role of labor supply receiving less consideration. We estimate the response of labor market flows to high-frequency changes in interest rates around FOMC announcements and Fed Chair speeches, and find that a contractionary monetary policy shock leads to a significant increase in labor supply: workers reduce the rate at which they quit jobs to nonemployment, and non-employed individuals increase their job-seeking behavior. These effects are quantitatively important: holding supply-driven labor market flows constant, the decline in employment from a contractionary monetary policy shock would be twice as large. To interpret our findings, we estimate a heterogeneous agent model with frictional labor markets and an active extensive margin of labor supply. The model rationalizes existing estimates of modest labor supply responses to idiosyncratic transfers with our new evidence of a large labor supply response to an aggregate shock.

articles.title: Juking the Stats: Policing, Misreporting, and Policy Evaluation
articles.abstract: We analyze a game-theoretic model of crime and crime reporting to study the quality of crime statistics. An offender potentially engages in illicit behavior; an enforcer chooses effort and how to report outcomes. Because of signaling concerns, the enforcer may misreport. We show that multiple equilibria can exist and characterize when crime is under- or overreported. Increasing the enforcer’s costs of data manipulation can backfire, increasing misreporting in crime statistics. When calculating treatment effects of parameter changes, the effect on reported statistics will not equal the effect on true statistics, and the true effect can be under- or overestimated.

articles.title: Freedom and Constraint
articles.abstract: A common objection to legalizing certain types of markets—in sex, organs, sorts of medical care—is that it would result in the coercion of some participants. But the general idea that expanding an agent's options can reduce his or her freedom strikes many as confused, and, indeed, its negation is taken as axiomatic in the formal literature on ranking opportunity sets in terms of freedom. In this paper, I motivate a general model of choice under constraints that is capable of capturing many philosophical concerns about the potential negative effects of menu expansion. Optimizing a preference relation subject to such constraints cannot in general be represented as unconstrained optimization of any binary relation. I then axiomatically characterize constraint‐sensitive generalizations of two prominent accounts of freedom. These characterizations provide proof of the possibility that menu expansion can reduce freedom within a disciplined generalization of the standard freedom ranking framework.

Reducing Health Inequality by Increasing Children's Education: A Two‐Generation Mediation Approach and Evidence from the United States
articles.authors: Liying Luo, Jiahui Xu, John Robert Warren, Kenneth M. Langa
articles.abstract: Recent research indicates that adult children's education may influence their parents’ health at older ages. However, a critical population‐level inequality question remains understudied: Would improving children's education increase or reduce parental health inequalities? To answer this cross‐generational inequality question, we analyze longitudinal data from the United States Health and Retirement Study using multilevel marginal structural models and well‐defined causal estimands. We find that educational inequalities in five parental health conditions would be reduced if their children obtained more education. In particular, the health disadvantages for the least educated (i.e., with less than 12 years of schooling) parents would decrease by 14–37 percent. Meanwhile, the health advantages for college‐educated parents do not seem to change. This reduction in health inequality is evident independent of how children's education is measured (e.g., the highest, lowest, average level, or based on a randomly picked child). We discuss two sociodemographic mechanisms—namely, the effect heterogeneity and distribution mechanism—through which the inequality reduction effects manifest. Our research joins a growing recognition of increasing education across generations as a strategy to improve population health and reduce health inequalities in the United States and elsewhere.

articles.title: Rethinking Fertility Responses to Armed Conflict: A Critical Review of Conflict–Fertility Research in Low‐ And Middle‐Income Countries
articles.authors: Victor Emmanuel, Emmanuel Olamijuwon, Katherine Keenan, Jo Mhairi Hale
articles.abstract: Current research on armed conflict and fertility has produced varied results, with some studies finding short‐term fertility declines and others observing subsequent rebounds. Drawing on 27 empirical studies from low‐ and middle‐income countries, this review assesses how conflict exposure is conceptualized and measured, evaluates the theoretical frameworks applied across the literature, and identifies pathways linking conflict to fertility outcomes. We find that established fertility theories were developed under assumptions of institutional stability that armed conflict systematically disrupts, and that no single theoretical framework is sufficient to explain the full range of conflict–fertility relationships documented in the literature. To clarify these pathways, we propose a multilevel conceptual framework connecting conflict to fertility outcomes, showing that seemingly contradictory findings arise because armed conflict operates through multiple simultaneous pathways at macro‐, meso‐, and micro‐levels that can suppress or accelerate fertility depending on conflict type, duration, and intensity. Lastly, the review identifies the risk of conflict exposure misclassification, particularly when recurrent low‐intensity violence is treated as a discrete shock, or when exposure measures ignore duration and proximity. Advancing research will require stronger theoretical grounding, more precise theory‐based measurement, and greater attention to whose reproductive intentions are being realized and under what conditions.

articles.title: The Demographic Impact of Leadership: Mayoral Education and COVID‐19 Excess Mortality in Italy
articles.authors: Francesco Mattioli, Alessandra Minello, Tommaso Nannicini
articles.abstract: During the COVID‐19 pandemic, excess mortality rose sharply across Europe, with striking territorial disparities even within countries. This paper examines whether the characteristics of locally elected officials influenced excess mortality in Italy—one of the first countries severely affected. Using weekly death statistics and a Bayesian hierarchical spatiotemporal model, we estimate excess mortality at the municipal level. To address endogeneity in political selection, we exploit close mayoral elections within a regression discontinuity design. Results show that college‐educated mayors significantly reduced excess mortality during the first wave by lowering both the likelihood and the rate of excess deaths, but not during the second wave. Analysis of newly collected large‐scale datasets on municipal policy activity and social media communication points to two possible channels: timely and more targeted local policy responses, and less alarmist, more guidance‐oriented public communication. Interpreting mayoral education as a proxy for broader leadership traits, such as rapid and non‐alarmist responses to crisis, the findings highlight how political selection can shape local demographic vulnerability and population resilience during acute mortality shocks.

Ideological (a‐)symmetries in moral judgments of online hate
articles.authors: Vladimir Bojarskich, Meltem Yucel, Lindsay Hahn, Tobias Rothmund
articles.abstract: Political ideology is key in how we react to social and political events, but how does it predict moral judgments of online hate? The contextual symmetry hypothesis suggests that conservatives and liberals condemn online hate similarly when it targets ideologically favored groups. The generalizable asymmetry hypothesis proposes that conservatives, compared to liberals, are less condemning of hate comments regardless of the target. Across experiments in Germany ( N = 903) and the United States ( N = 490), we found consistent evidence for the contextual symmetry account: Conservatives and liberals differ in their sensitivity toward online hate depending on the target and ground their moral judgments on perceptions of the aggressor's responsibility and the victim's vulnerability and suffering. These findings suggest that public divisions over hate speech regulation may reflect ideological differences in perceptions of victim vulnerability, suffering, and perpetrator responsibility, rather than a general conservative tendency to condone online hate.

articles.title: Education Policy in Multilevel Systems: Introducing the Index of Regional Powers in Education ( IRPE )
articles.authors: Johanna Schnabel, Steven Ballantyne, Anja Giudici, Paolo Dardanelli, Bethan Davies, Yordanka Dimcheva
articles.abstract: The distribution of powers over education policy is a deeply contested issue in many countries. While education is central to national economic and social agendas, it is also a policy domain in which regional governments play a prominent role in modern democracies. However, there is still limited knowledge on the extent of regional powers over education. While many indices only measure a country's overall level of regional powers, policy‐specific indicators do not distinguish between different dimensions of education policy shown to be politically relevant and to affect educational and societal outcomes. To provide a more detailed measure, this research note presents the Index of Regional Powers in Education (IRPE): A composite index that captures the powers of regions regarding three dimensions of education policy (distribution, stratification, content), focusing on primary and lower secondary education and access to pre‐school. Based on data from eight OECD countries with different forms of territorial governance, the research note illustrates, descriptively, cross‐country trends revealed by the IRPE. Regional powers tend to be higher in distribution and stratification, while content remains largely a central government power. The IRPE advances existing measures through stronger conceptualization and finer measurement and is scalable to wider contexts.

articles.title: Invisible Power: Local Officials' Informal Networks and Policy Diffusion
articles.authors: Yuhang He, Chao Pan, Dian Chen
articles.abstract: Policy diffusion research has primarily examined mechanisms such as geographic proximity, economic competition, and vertical pressure, while paying less attention to how the informal relationships in which local officials are embedded shape their attention to prior policy experience. This article focuses on birthplace‐based informal networks among principal local leaders. Using the adoption of open government data platforms across Chinese local administrative jurisdictions from 2012 to 2020, the article constructs a directed city‐pair‐year event history risk set, distinguishes between intergovernmental and interpersonal birthplace ties, and classifies these as strong or weak according to the spatial scope of shared birthplace. Each type of tie is positively associated with subsequent adoption when estimated separately. In the joint model, however, the most robust independent associations are concentrated in intergovernmental leader–place ties, and interpersonal ties add little once these are taken into account. Pooled interaction tests reveal limited heterogeneity across diffusion stages, levels of economic development, and administrative rank. These findings clarify the relational micro‐foundations of policy diffusion in the Chinese local administrative context.

articles.title: Punishment for Being Posh? Politicians’ Lifestyle Cues, Class Signals, and Voter Evaluations
Transnational Sexual Citizenships in a Fractured Landscape of Same-Sex Marriage: Flexible and Fragmented Rights for Queer Family Migration
articles.abstract: The legalization of same-sex marriage in a growing number of countries has opened the door for queer binational couples to pursue family reunification through spousal petitions. The global landscape of marriage equality, however, remains fractured, and transnational queer families must make strategic decisions to gain legal recognition of their relationship and immigrate together to live in one country. How does the piecemeal legalization of same-sex marriage shape queer families’ rights to pursue family migration? This article presents a conceptual framework of the varieties of transnational sexual citizenships to which queer binational couples can make claims. The typology is differentiated by the family and immigration laws of each spouse's homeland: flexible sexual citizenship; fragmented transnational citizenship; and sexual alienage. Interviews with queer binational couples seeking to immigrate to the United States show how couples consider the fractured legal landscape of family and immigration laws and then make claims for citizenship rights. Whereas couples whose homelands do not restrict family reunification by sexuality can choose where to settle and receive legal recognition, other couples have limited or no transnational mobility rights. Family formation decisions become claims-making steps, which comprise citizenship. Because family ties are foundational to making claims for citizenship rights, transnational queer families’ ability to move and live together remains stratified by both family and immigration laws. Findings highlight the family unit as a key axis of migration governance.

Public support for undermining executive accountability in times of crisis
articles.authors: Erica De Bruin, Calvert W. Jones
articles.abstract: Major crises have historically resulted in the expansion of executive power and undermining of democratic accountability. Yet, we know surprisingly little about which types of crises generate the greatest risk and which types of accountability-undermining actions – often justified by executives in the context of crisis – are most likely to gain public acceptance. To explore these questions, we field an original conjoint experiment over a large and nationally representative sample of Americans. Although respondents are generally averse to actions undermining accountability, they also reveal substantial variation in their degree of aversion – across both crisis and action types. We demonstrate that they are most likely to tolerate such actions after physical security crises, compared to socio-economic and political crises, and also most likely to tolerate actions undermining horizontal accountability, compared to vertical or diagonal. To the best of our knowledge, this research is the first to empirically demonstrate these hierarchies of risk, shedding light on how antecedent conditions as well as agentic choices can differentially shape public support for undermining executive accountability.

articles.title: Expert surveys and the ideational approach to populism: The impact of conceptualization and aggregation
articles.authors: Nina Wiesehomeier, Saskia P. Ruth-Lovell, Matthew Singer
articles.abstract: We contrast the conceptualization, operationalization, and measurement of party-level populism in three major expert survey projects: the Populism and Political Parties Expert Survey, the Political Representation, Executives, and Political Parties Survey, and the Varieties of Party Identity and Organization Survey (V-Party). Although all three adopt the ideational approach to populism, they differ in how the concept is translated into rating scales, the number and content of items, the specification of scale endpoints, and the aggregation procedures used to construct a single populism index. Drawing on 125 political parties from 23 European countries, we examine whether these methodological choices affect how parties are scored and how robust resulting rankings and classifications are to alternative aggregation rules. We compare each project’s original index with four weakest-link aggregation rules − minimum, multiplication, harmonic mean, and geometric mean − to assess the sensitivity of the resulting populism indices to compensatory versus non-compensatory aggregation assumptions. We find that aggregation choices can produce substantial differences, with the classical minimum function diverging most strongly from the original indices and from partially compensatory rules. While the most and least populist parties are identified consistently across aggregation methods, parties located in the middle of the scale are frequently reclassified, suggesting that methodological choices can matter most for empirically ‘intermediate’ cases. We further examine the inferential consequences by replicating a recent study, showing that aggregation rules can alter estimated relationships involving populist appeals, particularly when conclusions hinge on moderate, mainstream parties. We conclude with recommendations for the development and use of expert surveys.

articles.title: How municipalities organise policy implementation under weak enforcement
articles.abstract: Municipalities in Spain are subject to legal transparency requirements that are weakly enforced. This article examines how municipalities organise implementation under weak enforcement: how arrangements change over time, who takes responsibility and what prompts them to change. Drawing on 51 interviews with officers in charge of transparency in municipalities of varying sizes and compliance levels, we trace how implementation has evolved since 2010. We find that municipalities typically assign transparency duties to existing staff and structures, rather than creating dedicated roles. Although legal enactment often initiates implementation, moves towards more specialised arrangements are associated with external incentives, such as evaluations or rankings, rather than with legal enactment alone. Administrative and technical staff tend to drive implementation, although political backing often supports organisational change. Our findings suggest that weak enforcement matters not only for whether municipalities comply, but also for how they organise and prioritise implementation, allocating attention and resources among competing demands.

articles.title: Interpersonal trust in the policy advisory process: a research agenda
articles.abstract: Interpersonal trust is a key factor determining whether advice is taken into account in policy making, yet it has received little substantive attention in scholarship on policy advice and expert knowledge. Its role has only grown in importance amid accelerating democratic backsliding and the increased personalisation of politics in many jurisdictions. This article argues that policy scholarship can build on insights from other social science disciplines, which have a long-standing and rich tradition of researching trust, to develop a more purposeful and systematic approach to analysing interpersonal trust and its role in policy making. It sets out a research agenda for studying the phenomena that advances understanding of the informal dimensions of policy making, which have largely remained elusive. In doing so, it provides an analytical lens for examining policy making in settings characterised by weaker (or absent) democratic institutions, where interpersonal relationships may exert greater influence over policy decisions. Developing a stronger and more nuanced understanding of interpersonal trust is increasingly important given policy scholarship’s growing interest in non-democratic settings and the apparent erosion of democratic norms in many established democracies.

articles.title: Policy advisory systems and democratic governance in Italy
articles.authors: Maria Tullia Galanti, Andrea Lippi, Andrea Terlizzi
articles.abstract: Policy advisory systems (PASs) shape how governments organise and use expertise, yet their implications for democratic governance remain underexplored. This article examines how the governance of PASs influences democratic responsiveness and democratic accountability, asking how different organisational arrangements shape these core democratic dimensions. Focusing on the Italian PAS between 2020 and 2025, the article analyses how organisational analytical capacity mediates the relationship between democracy and technocracy. Drawing on a longitudinal case study of three governments, it discusses the consequences of the features and dynamics of the PAS (such as the creation of new advisory bodies, pluralisation, inclusiveness, adaptability, politicisation and elite circulation) on democratic governance. The findings show that these organisational arrangements can both enhance and constrain democratic responsiveness and accountability, depending on the institutional context and the inherited characteristics of the PAS. By linking PASs, policy analytical capacity and democratic governance, the article demonstrates how the governance of expertise shapes policy making and offers a framework for understanding when advisory systems strengthen or weaken democratic performance.

articles.title: Strategic Signaling: How Members of Congress Emphasize or Obfuscate Bipartisan Behavior
articles.abstract: Members of Congress engage in bipartisan behavior to varying degrees, yet their public messaging does not always align with their actions. This study examines why legislators strategically emphasize or obfuscate their bipartisan behavior in constituent communications. Using a new measure of bipartisan behavior based on original cosponsorship and a dataset of congressional e‐newsletters analyzed with OpenAI's embeddings model, I develop a messaging gap that captures the extent to which members (mis)represent their bipartisan legislative work. My findings reveal that party is crucial: Democrats tend to overstate their bipartisanship in messaging, while Republicans systematically downplay their bipartisan activities. Additionally, institutional differences matter. The partisan differences in how a member represents her bipartisan behavior are amplified in the Senate. These results highlight the strategic nature of congressional communication and suggest that legislators tailor their messaging to partisan expectations rather than accurately reflecting their legislative behavior.

articles.title: Species-Being and Praxis: Toward a Planetary Theory of Society
articles.abstract: This article argues that sociology has faced epistemic and normative crises since the 1970s, rooted in ontological amnesia inherited from Western modernity. Contemporary planetary ecological and social crises, alongside emerging epistemic challenges associated with artificial intelligence, expose the limits of this condition and underscore the need for an ontological reconstruction of sociology. I propose a theory of society as the praxis of species-being, grounded in ecological Marxism, feminist ethics of care, and decolonial-Indigenous ontologies. This theory reconceives the human as a historically reflexive, relational, ecological, symbolic, and temporal species-being. Social life emerges as the historically organized praxis of species-being through ecological structuration in historically contingent forms shaped by social practices, institutions, symbolic systems, and relations of power. The theory reorients sociological analysis by interpreting climate collapse, capitalist abstraction, linguistic erosion, and the breakdown of care as ontological fractures calling for renewed commitments to justice, freedom, meaning, critique, and solidarity.

articles.title: Beyond access: structural, social, and religious constraints on abortion in Rohingya refugee camps
articles.authors: Md Nuruzzaman Khan, Md Mashiur Rahman, Shimlin Jahan Khanam, Nipun Islam, Ananna Deb, Karen Block
articles.abstract: Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh continue to face major obstacles in accessing safe abortion care, despite its legal provision under the Menstrual Regulation policy and inclusion in humanitarian guidelines. This qualitative study, conducted in late 2024 and early 2025, explored how coercive forces shape abortion decision-making among Rohingya women in Bangladesh. Interviews with forty participants, including women, men, family members, community leaders, and service providers, revealed layered constraints across structural, community, household, and individual levels. Restrictive interpretations of law, policy gaps, and provider reluctance, driven by limited knowledge and fear of repercussions, restricted service access. Community surveillance, religious narratives condemning abortion, and patriarchal household control further narrowed women’s autonomy, while misinformation, stigma, and internal moral conflict discouraged care-seeking. These intersecting pressures often pushed women toward unsafe methods, increasing health risks. Addressing these challenges requires clearer guidance on service eligibility and sustained community engagement to dismantle coercive norms and reduce stigma.

articles.title: Elections, Expert Assessments and Public Sector Leaks: Evidence From a Survey Experiment
articles.abstract: Despite strong normative, professional and legal constraints, leaks of confidential information by public administrators continue to arise. Yet, data limitations restrict our knowledge about when such actions are most/least likely. Conceptualizing the decision to leak confidential information as a “bureaucratic dilemma,” we theorize that this decision is affected by election proximity and positive/negative expert assessments of policy proposals. We test the resulting theoretical propositions via a between‐subjects survey experiment among 1661 national public administrators in Norway. Our results reveal that impending elections reduce the perceived probability of leaks among public administrators who support government parties, while having the reverse effect among public administrators not supporting government parties. We also uncover that leaks become less—not more—likely when there is a negative expert assessment of a policy proposal (relative to a control group receiving no expert assessment). Our findings help elucidate the information‐sharing dilemmas faced by public administrators.

articles.title: Linking Women’s Equality With Government Integrity: Can Gender Budgeting Curb Corruption?
articles.authors: Marjorie De la Cruz, Milena I. Neshkova, Yoon‐Jung Choi
articles.abstract: Policies addressing gender inequality have increasingly been linked to more ethical governance, as women tend to be disproportionately burdened by corruption compared to men. One such policy is gender budgeting, an innovative approach to resource allocation that considers the impact of government spending on women and other underrepresented groups. Despite the growing popularity worldwide, we know little about its effectiveness in curbing corruption. This study evaluates the impact of gender budgeting on grand (political) and petty (bureaucratic) corruption using difference‐in‐differences estimations across a panel of 136 countries from 1980 to 2023. The results reveal a significant reduction in petty corruption, as gender budgeting improves the impartiality of public bureaucracies. Heterogeneity analyses also indicate a decrease in grand corruption, but only in countries with adequate levels of budget transparency, oversight, and public participation. The study highlights the far‐reaching consequences of gender reforms for the quality of governance.
