Uncertain Performance: How to Quantify Uncertainty and Draw Test Sets When Evaluating Classifiers
articles.abstract: Supervised machine learning has become increasingly popular in social science research, often employing classifiers to measure political constructs. Although evaluating classifiers on a test set is critical for establishing their validity, guidance on how to conduct such evaluation is limited. In particular, researchers have paid insufficient attention to the variance of performance metrics estimated on test sets. This article demonstrates that typically sized test sets yield highly noisy and often uninformative estimates of classifier performance, particularly for imbalanced tasks—common in social science applications like identifying hateful or emotional speech—where one outcome class is rare. To address this issue, this article introduces methods to quantify uncertainty in performance estimates based on their sampling distribution and validated with simulations. It also introduces a design-based approach in political science to enhance statistical precision when evaluating classifiers: efficient stratified sampling based on the outcome’s predicted probability. Simulations using synthetic and real data show that this strategy meaningfully reduces the variance of performance estimates, especially in imbalanced tasks, while ensuring that they remain consistent. Finally, the article illustrates how to calculate the test set size required to achieve a desired level of statistical precision. Accompanying statistical software enables researchers to easily implement these methods.

articles.title: Correcting Bias When Using Latent Regressors
articles.abstract: Many core concepts in political science are latent and therefore can only be measured with error. Measurement error in a predictor attenuates slope coefficient estimates in regression, often biasing them toward zero. We show that widely used strategies for correcting attenuation bias—including instrumental variables and the method of composition—are themselves biased when applied to latent regressors, often performing worse than simple regression ignoring the measurement error altogether. We derive a correlation-based correction using split-sample measurement strategies. Rather than assuming a particular estimation strategy for the latent trait, our approach is modular and can be easily deployed with a wide variety of latent-variable measurement strategies, including additive score, factor or machine-learning models; it requires no joint estimation while yielding consistent slopes under standard assumptions. Simulations and applications show stronger relationships after our correction, sometimes by as much as 50%. Open-source software implements the procedure. Results underscore that latent predictors demand tailored error correction; otherwise, conventional practice can exacerbate bias.

articles.title: Against the Grain: James C. Scott and the Narrowing of American Political Science
articles.abstract: This article traces James C. Scott’s intellectual journey against the grain of American political science. Drawing on his writing and my own work on the history of the discipline, I show how Scott’s interpretive approach diverged from the priorities of the National Science Foundation (NSF), the discipline’s dominant patron throughout his six-decade career. Whereas NSF-funded studies such as the World Values Survey sought universal metrics and cross-national comparability, Scott emphasized local knowledge and intersubjective meaning. In Seeing Like a State , Scott invited readers to turn his argument about the state’s compulsion for legibility against “a certain kind of reductive social science.” I take up his invitation, showing not only that the NSF privileged the types of legibility projects Scott critiqued but also that its efforts to remake the discipline bear a family resemblance to the pathologies of “high modernism.” A state agency elevated a narrow range of approaches as the authoritative form of political inquiry, entrenched an epistemological monoculture that devalued local knowledge, and “disciplined” a field uniquely positioned to produce knowledge critical of the state. This history illuminates enduring tensions between different modes of knowledge production and the cost of institutionalizing one at the expense of others. Scott’s early work, funded by the NSF in a rare exception to its orthodoxy, underscores the road not taken: a pluralist approach that could have nurtured other ways of seeing politics.

articles.title: Introduction: Swimming Against the Stream: James C. Scott and American Political Science
articles.abstract: American political science lost one of its most influential scholars on July 19, 2024. James C. Scott, Yale’s Sterling Professor Emeritus of Political Science, was not only a major figure within his home discipline. His work also shaped conversations across the social sciences and beyond, including anthropology, sociology, history, agrarian studies, geography, and Southeast Asian studies.

articles.title: Thinking about Names, Numbers, and Categories with James C. Scott
articles.abstract: Across his work, James C. Scott theorized naming and counting. This article explores potential links of those acts with category-making.

articles.title: Teaching James C. Scott’s Hidden Transcripts to Advanced Undergraduates
articles.abstract: In this essay, I recount how I used Hidden Transcripts to teach advanced undergraduates about different ways of understanding theory and evidence. Quotations from students’ research papers illustrate their use of Scott as well as his impact on their thinking and analysis. I hope in this way to honor Scott’s work and legacy—as a man whose voracious appetite for ideas stands as a model of the academic intellectual.

articles.title: Critical Hermeneutics, Shared Standards, and Scott’s Contrarianism
articles.abstract: If James C. Scott practiced an art of not being governed by the disciplinary standards of political science, then what type of art was this? What made it disruptive? And what are its implications for the science of political inquiry? This contribution to the symposium on his work addresses these questions via a reading of Weapons of the Weak: Everyday Forms of Peasant Resistance (Scott 1985). Although commentary on Weapons has noted that it is unusual for being an ethnography by a political scientist at a time when the discipline was headed in other directions, the book’s significance lies in its underlying concern to foreground meaning—which is to say, in its hermeneutic qualities.

articles.title: Two Cheers for Political Science: A Scottian Approach to the Discipline
articles.abstract: James C. Scott was famously and publicly skeptical not only of disciplinary boundaries but also of the very idea that he might be a political scientist. Even so, he not only served out his career in political science departments but also published (more than once!) in the flagship American Political Science Review. It is incontrovertible that late-in-life, anarchism-cheering Scott was a very different scholar from his more youthful, behavioralist self. As he shifted his analytical gaze from early postcolonial Malaysian bureaucrats to early-capitalist Malaysian peasants, and thence farther afield, his approach to power broadly changed. Yet, it would be a mistake—however much Scott himself might encourage it—to recast him as something other than a political scientist. Rather, his presence in the discipline confirms the breadth of what “counts” as political science, in ways both inherently intellectually fruitful and validating for area specialists and others who are keen to spread their scholarly wings.

articles.title: The Political Art of James C. Scott: Making Waves
articles.abstract: James C. Scott was a contrarian who questioned the benefits of strong states and who praised the political astuteness and agility of marginalized and impoverished people. He used metaphors, allegories, and legends to advance controversial ideas about the unpredictability of nature and society, the omnipresence of deception within governing institutions, and the secret political activities of downtrodden people. By drawing attention to wall graffiti, limericks, sidewalk gossip, and other phenomena seldom examined by political scientists, Scott’s art expanded and enriched the study of grassroots politics. However, he also neglected certain topics—including the forms of argumentation and the ways of listening—by which oppressed individuals transformed their heterogeneous opinions about circumstances, threats, and possibilities into common views, sentiments of solidarity, and springboards for collective action.

articles.title: A House Divided: Agricultural Producers’ Attitudes Toward International Trade
articles.authors: Evren Çelik Wiltse, Filip Viskupič, David L. Wiltse
articles.abstract: Trade policy in the United States began to change rapidly during the two Trump administrations as higher tariffs dominated policy agendas and voters increasingly favored protectionism over globalization. These protectionist tendencies may be easier to explain in sectors that experienced deindustrialization and offshoring. However, protectionism is more difficult to explain for sectors that greatly benefited from global trade. Agriculture in the United States stands out among the “winners” of globalization. Although farm incomes consistently increased due to the global markets, agricultural producers leaned heavily toward anti-trade candidates. To examine the nuances of preferences about international trade within the sector, we conducted a survey of agricultural producers in April 2022 in South Dakota. Results of a series of ordered logistic regression models with robust standard errors reveal that there was statistically significant variation among the farmers based on what they produced. We conclude that the “new” new trade theory is a good framework that captures this within-sector variation in trade preferences.

articles.authors: Lode De Waele, Kim Loyens, Caitlin McMullin
articles.abstract: This study examines how public managers shape intra-public hybridity when a reform requires two public organizations with different administrative traditions and professional orientations to integrate. We study the political and administrative integration of Flemish municipalities and Public Centres for Social Welfare (PCSWs), drawing on 35 interviews across 13 local government cases collected in 2018 and 2022. Using an institutional work perspective, we compare how actors used regulative, normative, and cultural-cognitive actions to integrate—or deliberately keep separate—structures, routines, and identities. The cases developed four hybrid forms: blended, segmented, segregated, and blocked. Blended cases were associated with institutionally broader combinations of work across organizational domains, whereas segmented and segregated cases showed more bounded efforts and blocked cases featured deliberate withholding of integrative work. These findings show that the same formal mandate can produce different organizational outcomes because local actors vary in the scope and combination of the work through which they enact it. The study advances a process-oriented account of intra-public hybridity and identifies deliberate withholding as a distinct mechanism of boundary maintenance.

articles.abstract: Under what circumstances do parties get a share of executive posts that is not directly proportional to their legislative seats? While there is strong empirical support for Gamson’s law, i.e., the distribution of executive posts in a coalition is directly proportional to the negotiating parties’ number of legislative seats, we know little about when deviations from this pattern occur. To get a grip on these deviations, we study coalition negotiations at the Dutch local level between 1998 and 2022. Major deviations from Gamson’s law are rare, and most deviations occur because no strictly proportional solution was available. Small parties are usually overrepresented and large parties are usually underrepresented. The norm of proportionality is very strong: divisor methods that distribute executive posts over parties according to their legislative seats help predict how these posts are distributed. There is no consistent evidence that parties’ bargaining power affects the direction or size of divergences.

articles.title: Environmental clash? The environmental dimension and electoral preferences in six European democracies
articles.authors: Silvia Bolgherini, Luca Carrieri, Matteo Giardiello
articles.abstract: The political debate over environmental issues in Europe has grown increasingly contested and likely influences voting behaviour. Yet most research treats environmental voting as a single environmental protection versus economic growth dichotomy. This article reconceptualises the “environmental issue” as a composite “environmental dimension” integrating socio-economic trade-offs concerning household consumption, public services, economic growth, and employment. We rely on original survey data from six EU member states (France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain and Sweden), testing the association between this composite dimension and the vote intentions for European party families. By performing logistic regression models separately for each party family, our findings yield two main results. First, anti-environmental attitudes are systematically correlated with the electoral preferences of Radical Right parties. Second, pro-environmental orientations are associated with voting intentions for Greens, Social-Democrats, Radical Left, and also Christian Democratic/Conservative parties. In brief, the environmental dimension generates widespread and two-sided electoral responses among supporters of different party families, constituting a significant correlate of their voting preferences.

Bayesian Estimation of a Spatial Dynamic Panel Data Probit Model
articles.authors: Xuan Xiao, Xingbai Xu, Dongxu Li
articles.abstract: This paper develops a spatial dynamic panel data probit model capturing spatial autocorrelation, temporal dynamics, and binary nonlinearity simultaneously. Given the complexity of the model, we propose a Bayesian estimation strategy based on Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. The approach allows for full posterior inference without relying on high-dimensional numerical optimization. To control for unobserved individual heterogeneity, the individual effects are modelled through a conditional prior that depends on the initial observed outcome and time-averaged covariates. Monte Carlo experiments demonstrate favourable finite-sample properties and accurate posterior uncertainty quantification. An empirical application to corporate merger and acquisition (M&A) decisions in the Chinese A-share market illustrates the usefulness of the framework for analysing binary decision-making in the presence of both network dependence and state dependence.

articles.title: Testing Hypotheses About Ratios of Linear Trend Slopes in Systems of Equations with a Focus on Tests of Equal Trend Ratios Tests of Equal Trend Ratios
articles.abstract: This paper develops inference methods for ratios of deterministic trend slopes in systems of pairs of time series. Cross-equation restrictions are considered with a focus on tests of equal trend ratios across pairs of series. Tests of equal ratios have been used in the climate literature for the empirical assessment of climate models by comparing trend ratios (amplification ratios) of model generated temperature series with those of observed temperature series. Because estimators of ratios can have poor finite sample properties when the trend slopes are small relative to variation around the trends, equal trend ratio tests are restated as products of trend slopes giving more robust inference. Asymptotic theory is used to generate critical values. Practical advice is provided for empirical practitioners based on finite sample performance. Tests of equal ratios are applied to five groups of observed global temperature series to assess alignment of amplification ratios across these groups of observed series.

Mirror worlds and misogyny: A mixed-methods analysis of incel discourse across mainstream and alt-tech platforms
articles.abstract: This article analyzes incel discourse as both an affective and ideological system across mainstream and alt-tech platforms, specifically Reddit and Incels.is. Drawing on a Computational Grounded Theory approach, I combine BERTopic modeling with qualitative thematic discourse analysis to examine how incel communities convert despair, humiliation, and rage into epistemic claims about gender, power, and justice. The analysis identifies three recurring formations: biologized rejection, the “foid” logic, and glorified violence, which persist across platforms despite stark differences in moderation and visibility. Building on Naomi Klein’s theory of the Mirror World, I argue that alt-tech spaces do not invent new ideologies but stabilize, intensify, and ritualize misogynistic extremism. Incel discourse is not merely descriptive; it is productive, ontologizing emotional pain and transforming grievance into knowledge through repetition, resonance, and digital infrastructures. Conceptualized as an affective epistemology, this system shows how misogyny is foundational, making violence feel not only imaginable but morally justified.

articles.title: The fringification of funding: Monetization strategies within the Italian anti-mainstream Telegramsphere
articles.authors: Giovanni Boccia Artieri, Stefano Brilli, Valeria Donato, Nicola Righetti, Elisabetta Zurovac
articles.abstract: This study examines monetization practices within the Italian anti- mainstream Telegramsphere. By situating these practices within the rise of Alt-Tech platforms and “fringification” dynamics, the article contributes to understanding how fringe publics sustain themselves. Based on a sample of 454 channels collected via Telegram’s “similar channels” feature, we investigated monetization methods, and the discursive frames used to legitimize them. We identified nine categories of monetization tools, along with a spectrum of rewards ranging from material incentives to intangible benefits. Five primary discursive frames shape administrators’ appeals for financial support: support independent knowledge, join the fight, support for demanding work, sense of belonging, and hacks and insider deals. While mainstream digital economy tools such as PayPal, crowdfunding, and merchandise sales dominate, it is the discursive framing—more than the payment method—that constructs oppositional identity and legitimizes funding.

articles.title: Conspirative nudge: Visual dynamics, far-right engagement, and alt-tech infrastructures on Telegram during Brazil’s 2022 election day
articles.authors: Elias C. Bitencourt, Paulo F. C. Fonseca, Eurico Matos, Letícia Cesarino, Leonardo F. Nascimento
articles.abstract: This study investigates how images circulated in Brazilian far-right Telegram groups during the 2022 presidential runoff. Combining transformer-based computer-vision clustering with qualitative analysis, we analysed 5,384 unique images within 78,032 visual messages across 373 public groups and channels, derived from an initial data set of 126,640 messages collected during election day. We identified four interconnected dynamics – synchronization of informational flows, segmented emotional mobilization, epistemic legitimacy fabrication, and creation of cross-platform repositories – that anchor visual practices within Telegram’s alt-tech infrastructure. These dynamics configure a sociotechnical environment we conceptualize as a conspirative nudge: a latent, distributed state of affairs that facilitates emergence of conspiratorial practices by rendering certain interpretations more temporally aligned, affectively resonant, and visually actionable. Our framework extends debates in political communication and platform studies by foregrounding how platform affordances and visual artefacts jointly enact conspiratorial environments beyond deliberate intervention.

articles.title: Ports of illiberalism: Cross-platform diffusion of far right, conspiratorial, and reactionary Rumble videos on Facebook
articles.authors: Fatima Gaw, Chloe R. Mortenson, Hoda Fakhari, Rod Abhari, Inaya Fatima Hussain, Ayse D. Lokmanoglu, Erik C. Nisbet
articles.abstract: Alt-tech platforms like Rumble are a critical part of the illiberal public sphere where extremist and ideological communities converge. Despite their seeming isolation, alt-tech content penetrates big-tech platforms through parallel ports—socio-technical conduits that promote illiberal politics among mainstream audiences. This study develops an expanded typology of parallel ports based on their differentiated roles in cross-platform diffusion and applies it to the actor network sharing Rumble video links on Facebook. Using content and network analysis, it traces the systematic sharing of the most engaged Rumble video links from 2022 to 2023, identifying the actors and communities that sustain the Rumble–Facebook pipeline. Findings show that primary ports drive social media engagement while horizontal peripheral ports maintain ideological cohesion as central actors in the co-sharing network. Vertical peripheral ports, while less central, provide upward amplification. We discuss how alt-tech illiberal content penetrates big-tech platforms and its evolution as platform content moderation weakens.

articles.title: Movement to mass-murder: Understanding online radicalisation in the alt-tech ecosystem through the ‘Passages’ of users from 4chan to 8chan
articles.abstract: This article explores mass user migrations between two alt-tech platforms: 4chan and 8chan, as a result of instances of perceived deplatforming surrounding Gamergate in 2014 and a series of mass-shootings in 2019. It finds that deplatforming can intensify online radicalisation by pushing prohibited behaviours and users to platforms more suited to their purposes and compounding commitments to what is prohibited. The article introduces the concept of ‘passages’ to help illustrate how migration events affect migrating parties and destination environments, showing that users embed their motivation for migration into their use of a novel environment in processes of environmental selection, ideational entrenchment and behavioural extension. Analysis is based on a large-scale study of 4chan’s ‘Politically Incorrect’ board, using mixed digital methods, which sees platform design and users’ interpretation of technocratic features work together to co-create structures of meaning, with platforms affording users particular features and users according platforms particular powers.

articles.title: Reappropriating the old platform: Nested alternative practices in Chinese alt-tech spaces
articles.abstract: Recent scholarship on alt-tech emphasizes two formation paths: secession outside the mainstream and contestation within it. Building on this, we articulate an untheorized pathway: subsistence within the legacy platform. Drawing upon Shove’s social practice theory and employing netnography with 32 interviews, we examine China’s Tieba. Findings indicate that nostalgia for past Internet practices anchors further practice. Core members utilize Tieba’s BBS architecture and governance to appropriate part of this nominally neutral platform into alternative discursive spaces. We conceptualize this path as nested alternativity: (1) structural nesting, or embedding communities deep within platform hierarchies to maintain low visibility; and (2) discursive nesting, or subsisting through political compliance while pushing sociocultural boundaries. This case study foregrounds alt-tech not merely as a site property, but as a practice property, especially where political and economic constraints limit options.

articles.title: Politics after persuasion: Reactionary politics in feed-based media environments – a conversation
articles.authors: Alan Finlayson, Robert Topinka, Marc Tuters, Eugenia Siapera
articles.abstract: This article examines the transformation of political communication in feed-based media environments through a conversation with Alan Finlayson and Rob Topinka. It argues that prevailing models of persuasion are insufficient for understanding contemporary digital politics, where participation, repetition, and alignment increasingly structure how meaning is encountered. Rather than focusing on the transmission of messages, the discussion highlights how platform infrastructures organize communicative environments that shape orientation, affect, and political identification. Within these conditions, reactionary political forms appear particularly well suited to the logics of visibility, antagonism, and engagement that characterize contemporary platforms. The conversation situates these developments in relation to media and cultural theory, emphasizing the role of communicative environments in shaping plausibility and belief. The article concludes by considering implications for platform governance, suggesting that regulatory approaches oriented toward discrete actors struggle to address forms of influence that operate through distributed and infrastructural dynamics.

articles.title: Alt-tech everywhere: From fringe platforms to infrastructural condition
articles.abstract: This special issue argues that so-called “alt-tech” has shifted from a fringe platform ecosystem into a broader infrastructural condition shaping contemporary political communication. While earlier research treated alt-tech as a parallel system emerging in response to mainstream content moderation, the contributions collected here show how its core logics—permissive governance, affective intensification, symbolic compression, and cross-platform circulation—now operate across the wider media environment. Drawing on cases from the United States, Europe, Latin America, and China, the issue demonstrates how alternative and mainstream infrastructures have become increasingly entangled, with practices and repertoires moving laterally across platforms. This transformation challenges models of political communication centered on persuasion and informational correction, foregrounding instead participation, alignment, and the infrastructural shaping of visibility. Under these conditions, political meaning is increasingly shaped by environments that privilege antagonism, repetition, and affective intensification.

articles.title: ‘Are we going the way of screwtube?’: Alt-tech imaginaries, platform infrastructuralization, and Rumble use during the 2024 US presidential election
articles.abstract: Alt-tech platforms constitute spaces of community building and ideological amplification for proponents of reactionary and far-right politics. As alt-tech platforms grow and scale, however, they can undergo infrastructural transformations—diversifying their operations while consolidating moderation, advertising, and governance practices. This can create tensions regarding user experiences and expectations of alt-tech. Drawing on a recursive, mixed-methods analysis of 76,280 user-generated replies to the videos of 3 leading pro-Trump influencers on the alt-tech platform Rumble in the period surrounding the 2024 US presidential election, this article describes how the ambits of alt-tech are discursively constituted in and through contestations over what can and should be done with media. Introducing the concept of alt-tech imaginaries to classify discursive articulations of the interests alt-tech platforms should serve, their proper relation(s) to authority, and the functionalities they should enable, the article addresses what happens when these ideas are confounded by infrastructural changes currently transforming Rumble.

articles.title: Deplatforming health misinformers: How telegram is leveraged to foster collective identity and shared purpose in the alt-health community
articles.authors: Nilou Davoudi, Jaigris Hodson, Victoria O’Meara
articles.abstract: As the COVID-19 pandemic raged, mainstream social media platforms like Facebook and Instagram attempted to curb the spread of health misinformation by deplatforming prominent groups that trade in conspiracy theories and “alt-health” misinformation. Telegram, known for its anti-censorship ethos, became an important alternative venue for this type of content and the groups that spread it. Through a case study analysis of one alt-health organization’s Telegram channel, this paper asks: What communicative tactics are used on Telegram to promote, legitimize, and grow alt-health organizations’ influence in the context of their deplatforming from mainstream social media? Four key findings are identified: (a) censorship is framed as a credential, rather than a social and political reprimand; (b) a politics of crisis is cultivated wherein democracy and freedom of speech are understood as subject to concerted and acute attack by powerful enemies; (c) elite collusion and corruption from governments and corporate actors are framed as pervasive; and (d) positive messaging cataloging wins and allied commentary from actors in traditional venues of power and authority are employed with increasing regularity over time. Taken together, we argue that deplatforming from mainstream social media and regrouping on alt-tech platforms such as Telegram offer specific sociotechnical and discursive opportunities that can be leveraged toward increasing legitimacy and epistemic authority for these organizations. Implications for the governance of social media with regard to health misinformation and conspiracy theories are discussed.

The populist radical right and the European Parliament's democracy promotion
articles.authors: Nea Solander, Karina Shyrokykh, Sonja Grimm
articles.abstract: Although the European Parliament (EP) is the democratic backbone of the European Union, its role as a democracy promoter is underexplored. This article examines whether and why Parliament composition, particularly the increasing presence of populist radical-right parties, affects the issuing of democracy resolutions vis-à-vis third countries. Analysing original data on resolutions issued between 2000 and 2020 towards 16 countries located in the European neighbourhood reveals that the EP largely acts in a value-driven manner, issuing democracy resolutions in response to changes in democracy. Increased populist radical-right parties' presence in the EP is, however, not associated with democracy resolutions, only when tied to issues central to their partisan agenda, most prominently migration. This suggests that populist radical-right parties' engagement with democracy promotion is not value-driven, but selective, intersecting with their core mobilising concerns.

articles.title: The role of issue salience and party polarization on framing effects: Evidence from EU public opinion formation
articles.abstract: How does party competition influence framing effects? This article explores how party politicization of the European Union (EU)—through issue salience and party polarization—influences the way citizens react to the content of frames. Using a vignette experiment on EU policy issues conducted during a legislative election campaign in Portugal, results suggest that issue salience limits framing effects by fostering a more autonomous process of opinion formation. Issue salience also shapes how party polarization influences public opinion. Party polarization moderates the effect of frames only on low-salience EU issues. In highly polarized contexts, individuals examine frames more attentively and are more likely to reject frames inconsistent with their prior beliefs, but only when issues lack salience. The findings help to understand how party competition influences public opinion formation.

articles.title: The moral infrastructure of financial markets: public regulatory discourse and the pillars of market justification
articles.abstract: Recent research on morality and financial regulation has focused on the role of moral reasoning in episodes of post-crisis regulation. Adopting a processual approach, this paper argues that moral reasoning continuously and dynamically shapes regulatory logic, even in ordinary times. Combining insights from pragmatic sociology and social research on financial markets, it claims that regulatory logic is structured by an imperative to sustain two “pillars of market justification”: the notions that financial markets are just and societally beneficial. Strains that undermine these pillars recur continually, yielding ongoing regulatory responses aimed at reestablishing justifiability in the pillars’ terms. Though these responses are subject to political controversy, the controversy itself is structured by the imperative to sustain the pillars. To demonstrate this, I analyze texts published by American regulatory agencies in 2016–2022, focusing on strains stemming from financial product complexity. The analysis illuminates the entanglement of morality, regulation, and political controversy.

articles.title: The Effects of Teacher Strikes on Compensation, Working Conditions, and Productivity
articles.authors: Melissa Arnold Lyon, Matthew A. Kraft, Matthew P. Steinberg
articles.abstract: We document the nature of teacher strikes in the United States and examine how they affect compensation, working conditions, and productivity using an original dataset of 745 teacher strikes between 2007 and 2024. The vast majority (89%) of strikes are motivated by compensation, and just over half are motivated by working conditions. We examine the impact of strikes on both strike aims and student achievement in an event study framework. The average strike leads to a 6% ($7,629) increase in combined annual wages and benefits and a 0.5 student (3.2%) decline in pupil–teacher ratios after 5 years. We find little evidence of sizable impacts on student achievement, on average, up to 5 years poststrike. Heterogeneity analyses suggest that strikes did cause student achievement to increase in districts with lower relative expenditures per pupil and in states where teacher strikes are illegal, both contexts where strikes achieved larger gains in teacher compensation. Math achievement declines in the short‐term after atypically long strikes, likely due to lost instructional time.

articles.title: Public Support for Environmental Aid: Evidence from a Conjoint Experiment in India
articles.authors: Elena V. McLean, Taehee Whang, Joonseok Yang
articles.abstract: Recent scholarship on foreign aid increasingly recognizes the importance of recipient countries’ citizens and their preferences. This is particularly relevant for environmental aid, which has grown substantially and produces both local and global benefits. We argue that public support for environmental aid projects reflects the extent of domestic involvement across the project life cycle. Identifying the most visible stages of aid projects—initiation, design, and implementation—we link local participation at each stage to public support. We test our expectations with a conjoint experiment in India using a realistic environmental project scenario. Support increases when projects respond to local needs at the initiation and design stages—particularly when they combine local and global environmental benefits—and when the recipient government cofinances project costs. In contrast, citizens do not distinguish among the domestic actors responsible for implementation: a null result that reflects indifference among domestic options rather than the irrelevance of local involvement.

articles.title: Dual-Use Discourse and Middle-Power Influence: The Netherlands in Global Climate Governance
articles.abstract: Global climate governance increasingly depends on actors beyond the largest emitters, whose commitments remain uneven amid domestic polarization and geopolitical rivalry. This article examines how European middle powers influence climate governance amid this context. It develops the concept of dual-use discourse: climate narratives crafted to project credibility in international arenas while managing domestic political and economic constraints. Through a hybrid discourse analysis of Dutch climate diplomacy across Rutte-III, Rutte-IV, and Schoof-I (2017–2025), the article examines speeches, policy documents, and parliamentary debates. The analysis shows how Dutch governments turn flood vulnerability and water-management expertise into diplomatic assets, while building climate niches around adaptation, circularity, and resilience. Such narratives also respond to coalition politics, legal pressures, sectoral interests, and public contestation at home. The article recasts middle-power climate influence as a fragile politics of credibility, sustained when narratives remain anchored in material capacities and credible implementation.

articles.title: A Break with “Business as Usual”? IMF Contradictions on Tackling Climate Change and What Are Seen (and Not Seen) as Viable Decarbonization Options
articles.abstract: This article explores the International Monetary Fund (IMF)’s economic ideas regarding tackling climate change. It unearths a broad repertoire of Fund climate policy thinking, fusing neoclassical “completing the market” ideas about carbon pricing with Keynesian or Schumpeterian calls for wide-ranging public policy interventionism. The resultant amalgam betrays cognitive dissonance, captured in the IMF’s climate policy trilemma, as the IMF highlights ecological “tipping points” and calls for dramatic decarbonizing transformations to “business as usual,” yet retains unwavering commitments to economic growth and fiscal discipline. Before 2025, navigating mandate restrictions, IMF climate policy mobilized around helping countries achieve Paris Agreement emissions reduction undertakings. Yet limited traction with governments, Fund knowledge limits, and ongoing contestation within mainstream climate economics hindered IMF efficacy. Fund climate policy efforts abruptly halted when a climate change–denying US president openly hostile to Bretton Woods institutions unleashed a period of “greenhushing,” sending climate policy within global economic governance into stealth mode.

Solidarity in Action: Evidence from the Gaza Student Encampments in Spring 2024
articles.abstract: In spring 2024, students established over a hundred Gaza solidarity encampments. We investigate how these movements should be understood in the context of a larger history of social movements, especially student movements. We present findings from interviews we conducted with students participating in seven encampments during the height of the student protests. Across our interviews, we observed students from diverse racial, religious, and gender backgrounds describing the formation of a community based on justice, peace, and humanity. Students made a concerted effort to connect histories in expressions of solidarity with people in Gaza, with other US movements, and with each other, particularly as a way to hold universities accountable and create their own democratic communities. We conclude with a reflection on how students’ descriptions of efforts to limit speech are troublesome for democracy, given that universities appear to be behaving in antidemocratic ways that have a larger impact on student learning, continued student political participation, and the ability of students to hold leadership accountable.

How Elite Communication Shapes the Emerging Politics of AI Regulation
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence is often treated as a legal or technical object of regulation. Yet whether meaningful regulation emerges will also depend on politics: how AI enters mass politics, which risks become salient to voters, and which elites are trusted to define the need for action before the issue hardens into a polarized partisan conflict. This article examines those early dynamics through a preregistered survey experiment with a behavioral component. We expose US respondents to competing media frames about AI’s risks and benefits, which are attributed to different elite sources. The findings show that the early politics of AI regulation is not organized around a simple pro- versus anti-regulation divide. Instead, it turns on the institutional form regulation takes, the uneven political legibility of different AI harms, and partisan differences in trusted messengers. Broad support for oversight coexists with sharper disagreement over whether government should lead, and elite cues matter differently across partisan groups. These patterns suggest that AI regulation remains politically open rather than fully sorted and that its future trajectory may depend on which harms, institutions, and messengers come to organize public debate.

Democracy in Hard Times
articles.abstract: Since the 1980s, in the transition from industrial societies’ party alignments, democratic Western knowledge societies have configured around a two-dimensional space, anchored by extreme left-libertarian and right-authoritarian political parties and structuring electorates primarily along lines of education and income. This configuration is now under strain posed by four challenges—technology and occupational structure, global security relations, demographic transition, and climate change—that are generating sharp societal disparities and divisions in an environment of slow economic growth. The politically most salient lines of conflict may shift from education and social class to occupational and gender divides, and the framing of conflicts may be more about political governance and citizenship than straightforward issues of economic distribution. The quality and the quantity (in fiscal terms) of the challenges and associated divides contribute to hard times for democracy itself.

articles.title: The Costs and Benefits of Guest Worker Programs: Experimental Evidence from the India-UAE Migration Corridor,
articles.authors: Suresh Naidu, Yaw Nyarko, Shing-Yi Wang
articles.abstract: We estimate the returns to temporary, legal migration using a randomized experiment with Indian applicants for construction jobs in the UAE. Individuals who migrate doubled their earnings. However, migrants paid substantial upfront costs to labor intermediaries and reported significant falls in well-being. We extrapolate linear marginal treatment effects for workers who declined the offer and find they would have similar pecuniary returns to migration but would experience larger drops in well-being. We estimate that accounting for the fall in well-being and the intermediary costs reduce the welfare gains of temporary migration to the UAE to one-half of the pecuniary gains alone.

articles.title: The Parenthood Penalty in Mental Health,
articles.authors: Alexander Ahammer, Ulrich Glogowsky, Martin Halla, Timo Hener
articles.abstract: Using Austrian and Danish administrative data, we examine the effects of parenthood on mental health equality. Parenthood imposes a greater long-run mental health burden on mothers than on fathers: the relative increase in mothers’ antidepressant prescriptions due to parenthood exceeds that of fathers by 97.6 percentage points (Austria) and 41.1 percentage points (Denmark). These parenthood penalties in mental health mainly reflect the demands of having and raising children rather than biology, relationship breakdown, or non-employment. Supporting this interpretation, we show that adoptive mothers encounter substantial penalties and also that employed, cohabiting mothers account for most of the increase in prescriptions. Given our results, one may call for interventions such as longer parental leave. However, additional quasi-experimental evidence demonstrates that such extensions increase rather than reduce the prevalence of mental health problems among mothers and thereby widen inequality.

articles.title: Residential (Im)Mobility in Traditional Working‐Class Areas of the Athens Metropolitan Area (2001–2021)
articles.authors: Thomas Maloutas, Stavros Nikiforos Spyrellis, George Kandylis, Iris Polyzou, Dimitra Siatitsa
articles.abstract: This paper investigates traditional working‐class municipalities in the Athens Metropolitan Area (AMA) over the past two decades, experiencing low residential mobility. These areas have moved towards the social middle of the city's socio‐ spatial hierarchy. Changes in their occupational profiles have been driven primarily by endogenous processes of social upgrading, supported by—declining but still strong and long‐established—family networks and homeownership, rather than by gentrification processes. These traditional working‐class areas have remained relatively unattractive to gentrifiers and, at the same time, inaccessible to poor immigrant groups, thus following a trajectory of urban change that differs from classic gentrification or pauperisation patterns. The paper brings to the front a contextual perspective helping to challenge the presumed universality of dominant urban change patterns. Moreover, the paper maps in detail local processes in traditional working‐class areas in a context of deindustrialisation, shrinking working‐class, and peripheralization of poverty, discussing how these processes affect segregation trends in the socio‐spatial hierarchy of the Athens Metropolitan Area. The methodology is based on detailed census data and on descriptive quantitative analyses.

articles.title: Remaking Futures Under Conditions of Temporariness: Aspirations Among Young Ukrainian Migrants in Times of Uncertainty
articles.abstract: The article examines how ‘protracted uncertainty’ shapes young Ukrainian migrants' planning horizons and aspirations concerning staying in Poland, returning to Ukraine or moving elsewhere. Bringing together scholarship on aspirations, temporality, and future‐oriented action, and drawing on 46 in‐depth interviews with migrants from Ukraine aged 18–35, it shows that war‐related uncertainty and legal and institutional temporariness orient aspirations towards short‐ and medium‐term horizons while keeping longer‐term spatial commitments provisional. The article makes three contributions. First, it further conceptualises ‘in‐betweenness’ as a strategic position from which young migrants kept several possible futures open across Poland, Ukraine and other potential destinations. Second, it identifies forms of ‘agency‐in‐waiting’, through which young migrants sustained and pursued aspirations despite unresolved settlement intentions. Third, it advances a spatiotemporal understanding of aspirations in displacement, demonstrating that temporal horizons and spatial commitments are negotiated together and that limited planning horizons coexist with active efforts to shape futures across places. In this way, the article shows how future‐oriented action is sustained without certainty about where or when longer‐term aspirations can be realised.

articles.title: Spatial Patterns and Hierarchical Classification: A Capital‐Structure Analysis of Migrant Residential Differentiation in Nanjing, China
articles.abstract: Understanding the residential segregation of internal migrants is crucial for achieving spatial equity in Chinese cities. Yet existing research tends to treat economic, social, and institutional factors separately, failing to fully explore their combined effects on the spatial distribution of migrants. Drawing on the housing pathways perspective, this study proposes a capital‐structure framework that conceptualises residential outcomes as the interaction between migrants' capital endowments and urban structural filters. Using sub‐district data from Nanjing, we operationalise this framework through a three‐dimensional ‘Cost‐Accessibility‐Network’ (CAN) indicator model and analyse it with principal component, cluster and decision‐tree methods. The analysis yields three key findings. First, spatial inequality among migrants is highly structured across sub‐districts ( D = 0.217; between‐district Theil = 99.9%). Second, we identify five distinct types of migrant residential environments. Third, and most importantly, the capital‐structure interplay manifests spatially as ‘spatial entanglement’: the primary differentiating dimension combines housing market filters (structure) and educational composition (capital), rather than being a pure measure of individual capital. Within this entangled structure, spatial opportunity further shapes higher‐scoring areas, while residential stability defines lower‐scoring areas. By providing an empirical typology of this capital‐structure entanglement, this study offers a replicable framework for understanding spatial inequality, with policy implications tailored to the distinct constraints of each residential type.

articles.title: Linked Lives, Migration and Social Mobility: A Family History Approach
articles.authors: Karen Anne S. Liao, Marta Bivand Erdal
articles.abstract: This paper develops a family history approach, grounded in the concept of linked lives, to analyse interactions between migration and social mobility. Drawing on 106 family history interviews in Hanoi, Manila, Karachi and Mumbai, we examine how migration, non‐migration and social mobility unfold within intergenerational families. The analysis shows that different family relationships matter at particular moments in social mobility trajectories, including not only parent‐child relationships but also siblings, extended kin and other relatives. Internal migration, residential mobility, international migration and periods of staying emerge as part of wider family efforts through which opportunities and resources, as well as constraints and costs, are managed across time. Attention to linked lives reveals how moving and staying, the maintenance of middle‐class positions, and responses to crises take shape within families across generations and places. Through family histories, we show how linked lives mediate the relationship between migration and social mobility over time.

articles.title: Sustaining democracy under the shadow of force
articles.authors: Zhaotian Luo, Adam Przeworski, Hongding Zhu
articles.abstract: Democracy faces two threats: incumbents may peacefully monopolize office, or political factions may seek power through violent conflict. Using a dynamic model, the authors examine some conditions under which democracy is sustainable against both threats. Two parties vie for office under the shadow of force. To resolve conflict, the incumbent can share revenue as well as hold competitive elections: each time, it chooses the probability of losing the next election and redistributes revenue. Elections enable the incumbent to concede control over revenue over time but come with regular risks of defeat. Democracy is sustainable if the economic stakes in elections are neither too low nor too high, while the military strength is sufficiently balanced between the two parties. When the stakes are high, democracy may be sustained only with civilian control of the military or programmatic transfers.

articles.title: The informational effects of institutional crowding: Evidence from zombie election monitors
articles.abstract: How do governments manage the political costs of scrutiny from international organizations? We introduce the concept of institutional crowding , whereby governments simultaneously affiliate with multiple international bodies sharing the same ostensible mandate but varying in capacity and value commitments. We develop this argument in the context of international election observation, where governments facing higher domestic electoral risk benefit from inviting not only credible election observation missions (EOMs) but also ‘zombie’ groups whose assessments are anticipated to be more lenient. The primary effects of this strategy are informational: When multiple EOMs are present, the resulting range of evaluations gives media greater latitude to present international assessments favorably, or to obscure negative findings behind conflicting signals. Using original media-based data on the presence and assessments of EOMs across 621 executive elections in 114 countries from 1998 to 2018, we show that governments facing greater domestic electoral risk — particularly where opposition strength is growing and previous elections sparked protests — are more likely to host multiple EOMs of varying quality. Notably, this pattern is not driven by autocracies alone, reflecting a broader political survival logic that cuts across regime types. Consistent with our theoretical mechanism, we show that elections hosting multiple EOMs are associated with more positive depictions of election observer assessments in the media, even as divergence among different missions increases. Beyond election observation, the logic of institutional crowding travels to any domain where institutional proliferation creates opportunities for information management.

articles.title: “My Religion Supports Abortion”: How Abortion Storytelling Supports Religious Freedom Challenges to State Abortion Bans
articles.abstract: Religious support for abortion was widely recognized in the 1960s and 1970s as outspoken Jewish and Christian clergy advocated for safe access to abortion prior to the 1973 United States Supreme Court decision, Roe v. Wade (Dirks and Relf 2017; Flowers 2018). After Roe , religious and moral arguments supporting abortion were supplanted in the public sphere by secular pro-choice arguments. At the same time, anti-abortion arguments became increasingly Christian due to the Religious Right’s mobilization around the issue (Balmer 2021; Schoen 2019; Sharma et al. 2017).

articles.title: Born to Govern or to Extract? Party Types Across Administrative Levels in Colombia
articles.abstract: Research on parties and corruption classifies them by ideology, while subnational studies set the party aside for the candidate. Indeed, organizational origin remains untested as a structured typology. I classify parties as traditional, personalistic, ethnic, rebel‐origin, or neo‐Pentecostal across three governmental levels. Operationalizing Attorney General prosecutorial records for 2011–2020, I build a composite corruption indicator for 1122 Colombian municipalities and estimate fixed effects, spatial, and regression discontinuity models. Rebel‐origin parties and citizen‐signature movements are associated with lower corruption, while traditional and personalistic types are indistinguishable. The ethnic category turns negative once parties whose origin and trajectory diverged are excluded, and tests of contested assignments strengthen the results. Voter turnout is positively associated with municipal corruption, a result that omitted variables do not account for. At the presidential level, however, party type loses significance. How a party was built, rather than its label, is therefore decisive for understanding municipal corruption.

articles.title: Resisting Epistemic Injustice and Unresponsive Regulation: Testimonies From Unmarried Couples
articles.abstract: Theoretical studies on responsive regulation and epistemic justice rarely examine how epistemic and regulatory dimensions operate together in administrative systems where citizens must (re‐)verify their eligibility for formally‐granted rights. In the case of Israel, despite extensive legal recognition of common‐law partnerships, unmarried couples face invasive verification demands and systematic credibility deficits that married couples bypass entirely. Epistemic injustice enables regulatory unresponsiveness by providing justification for fragmented bureaucracy and intrusive treatment, while unresponsive regulation actively reproduces epistemic injustice, positioning unmarried couples as less credible. Notwithstanding, rather than accepting marginalization, such couples resist by identifying alternative knowledge networks, documentation sources, and recognition frameworks. This article (i) demonstrates how epistemic injustice and regulatory unresponsiveness function as mutually constitutive forces in unmarried couples' lived experiences; (ii) theorizes unmarried couples' proactive epistemic resistance; and (iii) beyond the Israeli context, articulates design principles for more epistemically just responsive regulation that is grounded in participants' experiential and positional knowledge.

The Hype Versus the Reality of Generative AI in Elections: The Case of the 2024 Indian Elections
articles.abstract: The 2024 Indian General Election was defined by pervasive warnings that generative AI would unleash a tsunami of deepfakes and fundamentally destabilize democratic processes. To empirically test these predictions, we analyzed over 5.5 million messages from more than 6,000 WhatsApp groups, obtained through a large-scale data donation project in India. Our findings reveal a profound disconnect between pre-election hype and ground truth: generative AI constituted only about 1.1 percent of the image dataset once corrected for the measured recall of our detection pipeline, a figure we treat as a lower bound, with no evidence of a viral “deepfake” epidemic. Furthermore, a qualitative taxonomy of this content reveals that the technology was rarely deployed for deception. Instead, it was primarily utilized for “phatic” labor—automating the production of hyper-stylized “Good Morning” greetings, religious iconography, and patriotic art. We argue that AI adoption was constrained by technological friction and by economic incentives, as traditional “cheapfakes” remained comparatively more cost-effective alternatives for political actors. These results challenge the prevailing focus on the threat of AI-driven messaging, suggesting that the technology may not always lead to epistemic disruption, but rather to the efficient reproduction of existing social rituals.

articles.title: The Promises and Limits of Solutions Journalism: How Controversy Conditions Effects on Emotions and Attitudes in Response to News About Climate Change
articles.authors: Adam Shehata, Kim Andersen, Mats Ekström, Emil Östlund
articles.abstract: This study addresses an argument not considered in previous research on solutions journalism: that the emotional and attitudinal effects of solutions-focused news stories depend on the level of controversy of the solutions presented. Across two identically designed experiments focusing on reducing emissions from meat production (Study 1) and transportation (Study 2), we find that the promises of solutions journalism are conditioned by the real-world sociopolitical context in which it is embedded. Both levels of controversy and political predispositions among news consumers condition the effects of solutions journalism on the audience, even generating evidence of backfiring effects.

articles.title: What's Wrong With Claude's AI Constitution? The Limits of Corporate AI Self‐Governance
articles.abstract: Anthropic recently published a ‘constitution’ for its Claude AI model, a document that lays down ethical and other rules intended to make this AI behave well and avoid harms. In this paper I argue that this constitution is useful because it is couched in accessible language and anthropomorphizes Claude and so allows for comprehensive thinking about rules for AI. But I also argue that the constitution fails because it locates the ethics of Claude in the wrong place – an ethical all‐powerful being. In the paper, I argue AI should be understood as a large technological system that must be governed, like other systems with social consequences, across domains. Using the example of the mediated public arena, I show how AI functions as part of a media system – across content moderation, news, and democratic processes. In each case, it can be specified what kinds of rules are need for the proper functioning of the public arena. The paper concludes with more general reflections about how AI can be governed as a technological system, and how the ethical and social implications of AI should be conceptualized beyond ‘constitutions’.

articles.title: Exploring enhanced self-esteem reactivity in response to social prediction errors in adolescence
articles.authors: Klara Gregorova, Geert-Jan Will, Pia Burkard, Marcel Romanos, Andrea M. F. Reiter
articles.abstract: Self-esteem is a cornerstone of mental health across the lifespan. Throughout life, but particularly during adolescence, self-esteem is shaped by social appraisals. Previous work in adults has shown that momentary fluctuations in self-esteem are explained not only by whether we are liked by others but also by whether we are liked more or less than expected (social prediction errors). Here, we examine age-related differences in how social experiences shape self-esteem in 141 participants aged 10-40 years using an experimental social evaluation task and ecological momentary assessment. In the experiment, self-esteem reactivity to unexpected social feedback follows a non-linear age-related pattern, peaking in late adolescence. In daily life, self-esteem reactivity to perceived pleasantness of social interaction and naturalistic social prediction errors is stronger in younger participants. Individual differences in experimental and daily-life self-esteem reactivity are associated, highlighting heightened self-esteem malleability during adolescence.

articles.title: Sustained changes to urban mobility after COVID-19 reinforced socioeconomic inequalities in Argentina, Chile and Colombia
articles.authors: Carmen Cabrera, Miguel González-Leonardo, Andrea Nasuto, Ruth Neville, Francisco Rowe
articles.abstract: Urban mobility is central to economic activity, social inclusion and access to services. COVID-19 caused disruptions to mobility globally, yet its long-term impacts in Latin America remain poorly understood. Using > 170 million anonymised and aggregated location records from Meta-Facebook users in Argentina, Chile and Colombia (April 2020-May 2022), we examine changes in overall mobility volume relative to pre-pandemic baselines across socioeconomic and rural-urban gradients. Two years after the pandemic onset, mobility in the highest-density urban cores remained ~ 25–50% below baseline across the three countries, while the top 33% most affluent communities had not returned to baseline. These differences are explained by the scale of the initial mobility shock rather than by subsequent recovery rates. Our findings reveal how a global shock can entrench disparities in human mobility, with implications for urban resilience and planning in unequal nations. Our study underscores the need for proactive policies to prevent long-lasting mobility inequalities.

articles.title: City representation in Washington: determinants and responses
articles.abstract: When and why do cities lobby the federal government? Although intergovernmental lobbying has grown, variation in municipal lobbying remains insufficiently understood. We link city lobbying to congressional representation, arguing that poorly aligned cities hire lobbyists to compensate for representational shortfalls and that municipal competition can encourage lobbying when other local governments press competing claims. Using city-level data from 2008 to 2018, we find strong support for the alignment expectation and evidence that competition matters conditionally on a city’s position within the district, but little evidence that competition moderates the effect of city–members of Congress alignment. The results recast intergovernmental lobbying as both a substitute for weak ex ante representation and a strategy through which cities seek influence in shared congressional constituencies.

articles.title: A two-dimensional party-position panel from text and expert data
articles.abstract: This Data Descriptor releases an election-year panel of economic left-right and cultural cosmopolitan–traditionalist party positions for 708 parties in 65 countries from 1944 to 2025. The panel supports comparative analyses connecting party-level ideological supply to elections, regions, voters, institutions, or political economy over long periods. Estimates are produced by a Bayesian dynamic item-response model that places heterogeneous text and expert evidence on a common latent scale and reports posterior uncertainty for every party-election estimate. The model combines the temporal reach of manifesto and media text data with the precision of expert placements by treating expert surveys, manifesto codings, media sentence codings, and historical expert data as noisy item-level signals of underlying party positions. Text counts enter through a two-part hurdle binomial likelihood, aggregate expert means enter through beta-binomial likelihoods, general left-right ratings inform the relationship between dimensions, and party positions evolve through random walks within party segments. Technical validation combines item-response diagnostics, random and party-blocked held-out expert prediction, convergent and discriminant checks, posterior predictive coverage, evidence-composition balance, robustness analyses, and convergence diagnostics.

articles.title: Multimodal dataset of human driving behavior with vehicle dynamics, eye-tracking, heart rate and music
articles.authors: Sofia Sanchez-Mateo, Jose-Luis Tapia, Aranza Lira-Delcore, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia, Francisco Badea
articles.abstract: This dataset presents high-resolution, multimodal recordings of human driving behavior collected during real-world urban driving. Participants drove a defined urban route in a fully instrumented vehicle while physiological, behavioral, and vehicular signals were continuously recorded. The dataset includes eye-tracking measures, heart rate data, and a within-subject music versus no-music condition, reflecting typical driving environments. Vehicle dynamics were recorded through on-board signals, including steering angle, pedal inputs, and speed, complemented by GPS-based position and trajectory information. In addition, participants completed sociodemographic and driving-related questionnaires assessing habitual driving style, affective state, and self-perceived driving competence. Designed to offer a comprehensive representation of naturalistic driving, the dataset enables researchers to explore the interplay between perception, attention, cognitive load, and motor actions during real-world vehicle operations. Its multimodal structure supports applications in automated driving, cognitive and behavioral modeling, human-machine interaction, and the development of driver-state monitoring strategies.

articles.title: A High-Resolution Municipal Multi-Regional Input-Output Dataset for Korea, 2020
articles.authors: Haechan Lee, Jun-Ki Choi, Jiyong Eom, Hana Kim
articles.abstract: The official interregional input-output (IRIO) tables for Korea provide a consistent regional benchmark but are available only for 17 provinces and metropolitan cities. This study presents a municipality-level multi-regional input-output (MRIO) dataset for 2020, constructed from the official province-level IRIO tables and covering 229 local administrative units (Si, Gun, and Gu) and 76 harmonized sectors. The dataset includes a 17,404 × 17,404 domestic intermediate transaction matrix and accounts for total output, value added, final demand, and imports. Construction follows a sequential workflow: (1) construction of the initial seed matrix using municipal gross output by economic activity and the number of workers, (2) adjustment of intra-municipal transactions using Flegg’s location quotient (FLQ), (3) allocation of inter-municipal transactions using a gravity model, and (4) multi-regional generalized RAS (MR-GRAS) balancing to restore accounting consistency while preserving sign and zero patterns. The dataset is organized into modular files with metadata and construction code to support analyses of municipal production structures and inter-municipal economic linkages, as well as the development of environmental extensions.

articles.title: Managing Visibility in the Gray Zone: Quasi-Visibility and the Relational Practice of Algorithmic Resistance
articles.abstract: This article introduces the concept of quasi-visibility—a suspended, in-between condition that is neither fully visible nor entirely invisible—to challenge the binary presumption that has long dominated algorithmic visibility research. Drawing on textual analysis of 2,093 original Weibo posts and participant observation of the “naked child” incident, this study examines how algorithmic resistance unfolds under conditions of quasi-visibility. Our findings reveal two interconnected dimensions. In the actional dimension, users continuously recalibrate resistance through spatial appropriation and discursive maneuvering. In the relational dimension, they negotiate tensions with multiple actors through identity construction, boundary demarcation, and platform contestation. Theoretically, the article advances algorithmic resistance from a binary struggle “against invisibility” to a sustained practice of “managing visibility in the gray zone.” By foregrounding the lived experience of quasi-visibility, this study reveals how algorithmic resistance in China is not a unified collective act but a creative, sometimes concealed, and ambiguous political practice co-shaped by user groups, state censorship, platform governance, and the traffic economy.

articles.title: Correctness Costs Credibility? The Emotional Loop in AI-Powered Fact-Checking
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for fact-checking, but the role of emotion in this process remains unclear. We propose an Emotional Loop in LLM-based fact-checking, in which the emotional cues in user prompts influence model responses, while the emotional tone of those responses shapes users’ subsequent evaluations. Across three studies, we examine this process in the context of partially false claims. Study 1 audits four widely accessible LLMs across 24,000 responses and shows that emotional prompts—especially negative ones—can improve LLMs’ accuracy in identifying partially false claims while also increasing the emotional intensity of their outputs. Studies 2 and 3 ( N = 400 and 299, respectively) examine how users evaluate emotionally framed LLM fact-checks. Across both studies, these evaluations depended on users’ own emotions. In particular, negatively toned replies undermined perceived credibility among users experiencing negative emotion. Together, these findings reveal what we term a “correctness costs credibility” paradox in the Emotional Loop: Emotional input can sharpen fact-checking judgments, while emotional spillover into model output may reduce perceived credibility under certain conditions. The Emotional Loop offers a process account of how emotion operates throughout artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated verification, highlighting the importance of considering both model performance and user reception in LLM-based fact-checking.

articles.title: Representing Indigenous Peoples and Knowledge in the Study of Politics: Developing a Bibliography of Māori Politics Research by Māori Researchers
articles.authors: Lara Greaves, Mylia Kerehi-Ewington, Tohunga Riwai, Ella Morgan, Ben Barton, Sophie Rowland Newton, Annie Te One
articles.abstract: Many academic disciplines are on a journey to include Indigenous representation, decolonize, and indigenize. This paper represents efforts by a group of Māori researchers in political studies in Aotearoa New Zealand to create a bibliography of politics research by Māori researchers. The bibliography provides representation of the diverse ways Māori have conducted scholarship on politics. Overall, we found 696 sources, from 15 thematic categories. The results describe the different categories within the corpus of Māori politics scholarship, including those: stemming from mātauranga Māori (Māori ways of knowing) such as tikanga (customs) and tino rangatiratanga (sovereignty, self-determination); related to experiences of colonization (categories around founding documents, treaty settlements, and colonization); and works related to Western political studies disciplines (political theory; voter behavior; international relations). This represents an initial map of politics research by Māori and a useful framework for other scholars seeking to incorporate Indigenous works into their teaching and research.

articles.abstract: A carbon price is an effective and cost-efficient policy to mitigate emissions, yet low public acceptance and limited political support remain major barriers to its widespread implementation. This crowdsourced ‘many-designs’ project presents results from 55 behavioural interventions on real-world support for carbon pricing, independently developed by international research teams. By implementing all designs simultaneously with almost 20,000 US residents, this preregistered study shows very small positive but statistically significant effects of behavioural interventions on a set of design-specific proxies of real-world support (Cohen’s d = 0.06; 99.5% confidence interval (CI) 0.001 to 0.124) and on 4 out of 5 common measures of stated support (Cohen’s d values 0.06–0.08; 99.5% CIs from 0.006 to 0.112 and from 0.020 to 0.133; between 1.7 and 2.4 percentage points in increased support across outcomes), including the willingness to endorse a carbon price that internalizes the social costs of US$120 per ton of CO 2 emissions ( d = 0.06; 99.5% CI 0.012 to 0.118). Furthermore, the results reveal low-to-medium between-study heterogeneity ( τ = 0.07–0.12). Lastly, we identify strong overconfidence among research teams regarding the expected effects of their interventions and those of their peers, indicating a miscalibration of community expectations.

articles.authors: Lu Han, Stephan Heblich, Christopher Timmins, Yanos Zylberberg
articles.abstract: As urban populations grow, more people face extreme heat, increasing demand for natural cooling. Urban trees offer various amenities, including cooling benefits, yet their economic value is hard to quantify. This paper estimates the implicit value of urban trees by exploiting the emerald ash borer infestation of ash trees in Toronto as an exogenous shock. We find that a 1 percentage point increase in a postcode's tree cover raises property prices by 1.13 percent and reduces exposure to extreme heat, pollution, and energy consumption. These findings underscore trees as a cost-effective, practical strategy for mitigating urban warming. (JEL Q23, Q41, Q53, Q54, Q58, R11, R53)
