articles.abstract: We use close parliamentary elections as natural experiments to estimate the debt sensitivity of interest rates. Relative to an election in which one party barely secures a majority, an election in which no party achieves a majority causes the debt-to-GDP ratio to increase by 17 percentage points, while real interest rates rise by 99 basis points. If elections only impact real rates via debt, our results imply that a 1 percentage point increase in the debt-to-GDP ratio causes a 5.8 basis point increase in real rates, larger than most previous estimates. (JEL D72, E23, E43, E62, H63)

articles.title: Bonus Question: How Does Flexible Incentive Pay Affect Unemployment Dynamics?
articles.authors: Meghana Gaur, John Grigsby, Jonathon Hazell, Abdoulaye Ndiaye
articles.abstract: We introduce dynamic incentive contracts into a model of unemployment fluctuations. Our main result is that wage cyclicality from incentives does not affect the response of unemployment to productivity shocks. The response of unemployment is the same, to a first order, in two economies: one with flexible incentive pay and another with exogenously fixed wages. This equivalence is due to movements in effort. Under the optimal incentive contract, firms' profits do not change when wages fall because the effort of the worker falls too. (JEL E24, J24, J31, J41, J63, J64, L25)

articles.title: The Lasting Effects of Working While in School: A Long-Term Follow-Up
articles.authors: Mery Ferrando, Noemí Katzkowicz, Thomas Le Barbanchon, Diego Ubfal
articles.abstract: This paper provides the first experimental evidence on the long-term effects of work-study programs, leveraging a randomized lottery design from a national program in Uruguay. Participation leads to a persistent 11 percent increase in formal labor earnings seven years after the program, driven by a 4 percent increase in the monthly probability of being employed and a 6 percent increase in monthly wages. Effects are significantly larger for men, while remaining positive for women. The program is highly cost-effective, outperforming most job training programs and reaching levels comparable to early-childhood investments. (JEL D44, I21, I26, J13, J24, J31, O15)

articles.title: Measuring Sensitive Outcomes through Ballot Bag Surveys
articles.authors: Bruno Crépon, Ahmed Elsayed, Jules Gazeaud
articles.abstract: Prevailing methods for measuring sensitive outcomes confront researchers with an inherent bias-variance trade-off: Direct questioning is prone to a sensitivity bias, while indirect methods such as list experiments are substantially less precise. We test the ballot bag, a novel technique that relaxes this trade-off by mitigating bias in direct questioning while improving precision over indirect methods. In an experiment in Egypt, where direct questions on irregular migration are biased, ballot bag estimates are not statistically different from a list experiment but exhibit lower variance. Consequently, treatment effects are highly significant via the ballot bag and not via the list experiment. (JEL C83, C93, E24, J61, K37, L25, O15)

articles.title: Rules versus Discretion without Common Knowledge
articles.abstract: This paper revisits the classical time-inconsistent problem à la Barro and Gordon (1983) while relaxing the common knowledge assumption. When information is complete, achieving the first-best outcome is not possible, and the welfare under committed rules surpasses that under discretion. In contrast, without common knowledge, a policymaker adhering to committed rules can always attain the first-best outcome. If a commitment device is unavailable, the resulting welfare loss can either increase or decrease relative to the common knowledge benchmark. (JEL D83, E60)

articles.title: The Missing Poor
articles.authors: Torsten Figueiredo Walter, Niclas Moneke, Ana Radu
articles.abstract: Population censuses constitute the basis of public resource allocation and political representation. This paper shows that census forms commonly generate incentives for enumerators to disproportionately omit members of larger households. Using microdata from 254 censuses, we estimate that this leads to undercounting in at least 60 percent of censuses. Omission is concentrated in poor countries where 0.6 percent of the population is missing. Within countries, poor households are missing three times as many members as rich ones, leading to larger undercounts in poorer regions. We illustrate how this translates into underfunding of public services and political underrepresentation in poor regions. (JEL C81, D72, I32, J11, O12)

articles.title: Ten Years of Relational Power: The Long-Run Effects of Teaching Negotiation Skills to Adolescent Girls
articles.authors: Nava Ashraf, Natalie Bau, Corinne Low, Xiaoyue Shan
articles.abstract: We evaluate the effects of teaching negotiation skills to adolescent girls in economically vulnerable communities in Lusaka, Zambia, ten years later. Treated participants complete 0.23 more years of education. Consistent with greater relational empowerment, they also begin sexual activity later, have smaller age gaps with their husbands, and express less traditional gender attitudes. Using a surrogate approach, social benefits and costs from increased education alone suggest that the intervention generated 7.6 dollars for every dollar spent and had a very high marginal value of public funds of 10.5. (JEL I12, I21, I26, J13, J16, J24, O15)

articles.title: Household-Level Responses to the European Energy Crisis
articles.authors: Lassi Ahlvik, Tuomas Kaariaho, Matti Liski, Iivo Vehviläinen
articles.abstract: Cost-of-living shocks can have large and unequal effects, but causal evidence on households' adaptive responses is scarce. Using Finnish administrative microdata from the 2022 energy crisis, we exploit variation in electricity contract expirations to identify behavioral responses in electricity use, labor earnings, financial distress, and residual consumption and savings. We find notable heterogeneity in responses that shape the final incidence: High-income households primarily reduced electricity consumption, while low-income households reduced consumption less, responding instead through increased labor supply, more payment defaults, and cutbacks in spending and savings. Longer anticipation softens but does not eliminate these impacts. (JEL D12, D91, G51, J22, J31, L94, Q41)
